knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compactness converts normalized approximate normals into an exact limiting-normal balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated assumptions, there exist a subsequence \((k_j)\) and vectors \(x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\), for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), such that
\[
x_{i,k_j}^*\to x_i^*,\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0,\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m\lVert x_i^*\rVert=1.
\]
Thus the normalized approximate normal relations admit a nontrivial exact limiting-normal relation at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, normalized and asymptotically balanced nearby Fréchet normals have a subsequence converging to nonzero limiting normals at the reference point whose sum is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\).
For each \(k\), points \(x_{ik}\to\bar x\) and Fréchet normals \(x_{ik}^*\in\widehat N_{\Omega_i}(x_{ik})\) satisfy \(\sum_i\lVert x_{ik}^*\rVert=1\) and \(\lVert\sum_i x_{ik}^*\rVert\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After passage to a subsequence, \(x_{ik}^*\to x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\), \(\sum_i\lVert x_i^*\rVert=1\), and \(\sum_i x_i^*=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Normal Cone from Limiting Normalized Perpendicular Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional representation at a closure point of an arbitrary set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X$ be finite-dimensional, let $C\subset X$, and let $x\in\operatorname{cl}C$. Then $N_C(x)$ is the closed convex cone generated by
\[
\{0\}\cup\left\{v:\ v=\lim_{i\to\infty}\frac{v_i}{\lVert v_i\rVert},\ v_i\perp C\text{ at }x_i,\ x_i\to x,\ v_i\to0\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a closure point of a set in a finite-dimensional space, the Clarke normal cone is the closed convex cone generated by the origin and the limiting normalized perpendicular directions described in the proposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_C(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\!\left(\{0\}\cup\left\{v:\ v=\lim_i v_i/\lVert v_i\rVert,\ v_i\perp C\text{ at }x_i,\ x_i\to x,\ v_i\to0\right\}\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient-Limsup Representation of the Clarke Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional representation derived under the local Lipschitz and null-set hypotheses of the accompanying generalized-gradient theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be Lipschitz near \(x\), let \(S\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) have Lebesgue measure zero, and let \(\Omega_f\) be the nondifferentiability set of \(f\). Then, for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
f^{\circ}(x;v)=\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\y\notin S\cup\Omega_f}}\nabla f(y)\cdot v.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every direction v, the Clarke directional derivative at x equals the upper limit of gradient-direction products over differentiability points approaching x while avoiding any prescribed null set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^{\circ}(x;v)=\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\y\notin S\cup\Omega_f}}\nabla f(y)\cdot v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perpendicular Vector to a Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-based definition of a nonzero perpendicular direction at a point in the set closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), \(x\in\operatorname{cl}C\), and \(v\ne0\). The vector \(v\) is perpendicular to \(C\) at \(x\), written \(v\perp C\) at \(x\), if there exists \(x'\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(v=x'-x\) and \(x\) is the unique closest point in \(\operatorname{cl}C\) to \(x'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero vector v is perpendicular to C at x when it points from x to a point x' for which x is the unique closest point in the closure of C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\perp C\text{ at }x\iff\exists x'\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ v=x'-x\ \text{ and }\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in\operatorname{cl}C}\lVert x'-c\rVert=\{x\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint Lipschitz hypothesis for a finite-dimensional parameterized maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single finite-dimensional condition subsuming the basic compactness, continuity, and uniform-Lipschitz assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $T$ be a compact subset of a finite-dimensional Banach space $Y$. For some $\varepsilon>0$, suppose that for all $t_1,t_2\in T+2\varepsilon B_Y$ and all $x_1,x_2\in U$,
\[|\phi(t_1,x_1)-\phi(t_2,x_2)|\le K\bigl(\|t_1-t_2\|_Y+\|x_1-x_2\|_X\bigr).\]
This joint Lipschitz condition supplies the compactness, parameter-continuity, common local Lipschitz, boundedness, and metrizability hypotheses used for the parameterized maximum calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the parameter set is compact in a finite-dimensional Banach space and the parameterized function is jointly K-Lipschitz on a fixed enlargement of that set and on U, this single condition provides the basic hypotheses needed for the pointwise-maximum calculus.
assumptions_latex: T\subset Y\text{ is compact and }\dim Y<\infty
\forall t_1,t_2\in T+2\varepsilon B_Y,\ \forall x_1,x_2\in U,\quad |\phi(t_1,x_1)-\phi(t_2,x_2)|\le K(\|t_1-t_2\|_Y+\|x_1-x_2\|_X)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The joint Lipschitz condition subsumes hypotheses (i)--(iii) and the stated metrizability alternative for the parameterized maximum calculus.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance Characterization of Interior Clarke Tangent Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform local characterization for a closed Euclidean set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $C\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be closed and let $x\in C$. Then
\[
v\in\operatorname{int}T_C(x)
\iff
\exists\varepsilon>0\ \text{such that}\ d_C(y+tw)\le d_C(y)
\]
for all $y\in x+\varepsilon B$, $w\in v+\varepsilon B$, and $t\in[0,\varepsilon)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector lies in the interior of the Clarke tangent cone exactly when, uniformly over sufficiently small perturbations of the base point and direction, every sufficiently small nonnegative step does not increase the distance to the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\in\operatorname{int}T_C(x)\iff\exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall y\in x+\varepsilon B\ \forall w\in v+\varepsilon B\ \forall t\in[0,\varepsilon):\ d_C(y+tw)\le d_C(y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Inequality for a Perpendicular Vector
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global quadratic estimate induced by a projection-generated perpendicular direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(x\in\operatorname{cl}C\), and suppose \(v\perp C\) at \(x\). Then, for every \(c\in\operatorname{cl}C\),
\[
\langle v,c-x\rangle\leq\frac12\lVert x-c\rVert^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector perpendicular to C at x satisfies a quadratic upper bound on its inner product with every displacement from x to a point in the closure of C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall c\in\operatorname{cl}C,\quad\langle v,c-x\rangle\leq\frac12\lVert x-c\rVert^2

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\) be Lipschitz on a convex neighborhood \(U\times V\) of \((\alpha,\beta)\). Suppose that, for every \(\alpha'\) near \(\alpha\), the function \(f(\alpha',\cdot)\) is convex on \(V\). Then
\[
(z,w)\in\partial f(\alpha,\beta)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad w\in\partial_2f(\alpha,�beta).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is locally Lipschitz and locally convex in its second variable block, the second component of every Clarke generalized gradient belongs to the partial subdifferential in that block.

children.title: Asplund-Space Regime
children.top_down_role: Limiting and fuzzy generalized differentiation in Asplund spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund Banach space, and \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in\bigcap_i\Omega_i\).
The family is locally extremal at \(\bar x\): arbitrarily small translations make its members locally disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there are \(x_i\in\Omega_i\cap B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) and \(x_i^*\in\widehat N_{\Omega_i}(x_i)\) with \(\sum_i\|x_i^*\|=1\) and \(\|\sum_i x_i^*\|<\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fuzzy Fréchet-normal extremal principle in an Asplund ambient space.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Extremal Principle in Asplund Spaces p. 180
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), one can choose points \(x_i\in\Omega_i\cap B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) and Fréchet normals \(x_i^*\in\widehat N_{\Omega_i}(x_i)\) such that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i^*\|=1
\quad\text{and}\quad
\left\|\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*\right\|<\varepsilon.
\]
The points and normals may depend on \(\varepsilon\); the conclusion is therefore fuzzy rather than an exact Fréchet-normal relation at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local extremality in an Asplund space produces normalized Fréchet normals at nearby points whose sum is arbitrarily small.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Decentralized Equilibrium via Nonlinear Prices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the baseline differentiable conclusion from the conditional smooth, unique-extremum, and convex-concave refinements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \varepsilon>0 and assume the hypotheses of Theorem 8.5. Then there exist a suboptimal triple (x,y,w) satisfying the stated \varepsilon/2-proximity conditions, a price p^*\in E^*\setminus\{0\} satisfying p^*\in\widehat N(w;\operatorname{cl}W)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^* and  rac{1-\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{n+m+1}}\leq\|p^*\|\leq rac{1+\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{n+m+1}}, and real-valued functions g_i and h_1,\ldots,h_{m+1} on E. Each g_i is Frechet differentiable at x_i and attains a global minimum over \operatorname{cl}P_i( ar x) at x_i; each h_j, j=1,\ldots,m, is Frechet differentiable at y_j and attains a global maximum over \operatorname{cl}S_j at y_j; and h_{m+1} is Frechet differentiable at w and attains a global maximum over \operatorname{cl}W at w. They satisfy \|
abla g_i(x_i)-p^*\|\leq\varepsilon, \|
abla h_j(y_j)-p^*\|\leq\varepsilon, and \|
abla h_{m+1}(w)-p^*\|\leq\varepsilon. If E admits an \mathcal S	ext{-smooth bump function of the stipulated class}, the functions may be chosen \mathcal S	ext{-smooth} with all these extrema unique. Under that refinement, if E also admits a Frechet-smooth renorm, the g_i may be chosen convex and the h_j concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The approximate welfare hypotheses yield a nearby suboptimal triple and differentiable nonlinear price functions whose gradients approximate a common nonzero marginal price and globally decentralize the triple. A suitable smooth bump function permits globally smooth functions with unique extrema; smooth renormability additionally permits convex consumer functions and concave producer and feasibility functions.
assumptions_latex: E\text{ admits an }\mathcal S\text{-smooth bump function only for the smooth unique-extremum refinement}
E\text{ admits a Frechet-smooth renorm only for the convex-concave refinement}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(x,y,w),\ p^*\neq0,\ (g_i),\ (h_j)\text{ satisfying the stated price, gradient-approximation, and global-extremum properties, with the additional conclusions only under their respective hypotheses.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Extended Second Welfare Theorem in an Asplund Commodity Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired Pareto and weak-Pareto versions under their respective net-demand qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (\bar x,\bar y) be a local Pareto (respectively, local weak-Pareto) optimal allocation of an economy with Asplund commodity space E, and assume the net-demand qualification condition (respectively, the net-demand weak qualification condition) at (\bar x,\bar y). For every \varepsilon>0 there exist a suboptimal triple (x,y,w)\in\prod_{i=1}^n\operatorname{cl}P_i(\bar x)\times\prod_{j=1}^m\operatorname{cl}S_j\times\operatorname{cl}W, with w defined by the economy's feasibility construction, and p^*\in E^*\setminus\{0\} such that x_i\in\bar x_i+(\varepsilon/2)\mathbb B, y_j\in\bar y_j+(\varepsilon/2)\mathbb B, and w\in\bar w+(\varepsilon/2)\mathbb B; moreover, -p^*\in\widehat N(x_i;\operatorname{cl}P_i(\bar x))+\varepsilon\mathbb B^* for every i, p^*\in\widehat N(y_j;\operatorname{cl}S_j)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^* for every j, p^*\in\widehat N(w;\operatorname{cl}W)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*, and \frac{1-\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{n+m+1}}\leq\|p^*\|\leq\frac{1+\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{n+m+1}}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the corresponding net-demand qualification, every locally Pareto-optimal or weak-Pareto-optimal allocation in an Asplund commodity space admits, for each positive tolerance, a nearby suboptimal triple and a common nonzero marginal price satisfying approximate regular-normal conditions and the stated norm bounds.
assumptions_latex: E\text{ is an Asplund commodity space}
(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is locally Pareto optimal, or locally weak-Pareto optimal}
\text{The corresponding net-demand qualification condition holds at }(\bar x,\bar y)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(x,y,w),\ p^*\in E^*\setminus\{0\}\text{ satisfying the stated proximity, approximate regular-normal, and norm conditions.}

\[

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Prenormal structure on a Banach space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes off-set emptiness, locality with respect to the set germ, and the approximate two-set normal-separation axiom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space. A prenormal structure assigns to every nonempty \(\Omega\subset X\) a mapping \(\widehat{\mathcal N}(\cdot;\Omega):X\rightrightarrows X^*\) such that \(\widehat{\mathcal N}(x;\Omega)=\varnothing\) for \(x\notin\Omega\), and \(\widehat{\mathcal N}(x;\Omega)=\widehat{\mathcal N}(x;\widetilde\Omega)\) whenever \(\Omega\) and \(\widetilde\Omega\) coincide near \(x\in\Omega\). It also satisfies: for every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), every \(a\in X\) with \(\|a\|\leq\varepsilon\), and closed sets \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\), if \((\bar x_1,\bar x_2)\) is a local minimizer on \(\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\) of \(\psi(x_1,x_2)=\|x_1-x_2+a\|+\varepsilon(\|x_1-\bar x_1\|+\|x_2-\bar x_2\|)\) and \(\bar x_1-\bar x_2+a\neq0\), then there exist \(\widetilde x_i\in\bar x_i+\varepsilon\mathbb B\), \(i=1,2\), and \(x^*\in X^*\) with \(\|x^*\|=1\) such that \((-x^*,x^*)\in\widehat{\mathcal N}(\widetilde x_1;\Omega_1)\times\widehat{\mathcal N}(\widetilde x_2;\Omega_2)+\gamma(\mathbb B^*\times\mathbb B^*)\) for every \(\gamma>\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prenormal structure is a local set-normal mapping, empty outside the set, that satisfies the stated approximate two-set normal-separation condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\widetilde x_i\in\bar x_i+\varepsilon\mathbb B,\ \exists x^*\in X^*,\ \|x^*\|=1:\ \forall\gamma>\varepsilon,\ (-x^*,x^*)\in\widehat{\mathcal N}(\widetilde x_1;\Omega_1)\times\widehat{\mathcal N}(\widetilde x_2;\Omega_2)+\gamma(\mathbb B^*\times\mathbb B^*)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Abstract extremal principle for a prenormal structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate prenormal separation and SNC-dependent limiting separation for an extremal system of two closed sets in a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{\Omega_1,\Omega_2,\bar x\}\) be an extremal system of closed sets in a Banach space \(X\), and let \(\widehat{\mathcal N}\) define a prenormal structure on \(X\). Then: (i) for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(x_i\in\Omega_i\cap(\bar x+\varepsilon\mathbb B)\), \(i=1,2\), and \(x^*\in X^*\) with \(\|x^*\|=1\) such that \[x^*\in\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal N}(x_1;\Omega_1)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*\bigr)\cap\bigl(-\widehat{\mathcal N}(x_2;\Omega_2)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*\bigr).\] (ii) If one of \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\) is \(\widehat{\mathcal N}\)-sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\), then there exists \(x^*\in\mathbb B^*\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[x^*\in\overline{\mathcal N}(\bar x;\Omega_1)\cap\bigl(-\overline{\mathcal N}(\bar x;\Omega_2)\bigr),\] where \(\overline{\mathcal N}\) is the generated topological normal structure. If, in addition, \(\mathbb B^*\subset X^*\) is weak-star sequentially compact, then there exists \(x^*\in\mathbb B^*\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[x^*\in\mathcal N(\bar x;\Omega_1)\cap\bigl(-\mathcal N(\bar x;\Omega_2)\bigr),\] where \(\mathcal N\) is the generated sequential normal structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every two-set extremal system admits arbitrarily accurate nearby opposing prenormal certificates. If either set is sequentially normally compact, a nonzero opposing topological-normal certificate exists at the reference point; if the dual ball is also weak-star sequentially compact, a nonzero opposing sequential-normal certificate exists.
assumptions_latex: \widehat{\mathcal N}\text{ defines a prenormal structure on }X
\text{For the topological-normal conclusion, one of }\Omega_1,\Omega_2\text{ is }\widehat{\mathcal N}\text{-SNC at }\bar x
\text{For the sequential-normal conclusion, additionally }\mathbb B^*\subset X^*\text{ is weak* sequentially compact}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists x_1,x_2,x^*\text{ satisfying the approximate opposing-prenormal inclusion};\quad \widehat{\mathcal N}\text{-SNC of one set}\Longrightarrow\exists x^*\in\mathbb B^*\setminus\{0\}\text{ in the opposing topological normals};\quad \widehat{\mathcal N}\text{-SNC and weak* sequential compactness of }\mathbb B^*\Longrightarrow\exists x^*\in\mathbb B^*\setminus\{0\}\text{ in the opposing sequential normals}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon, approximate, and exact extremal principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines three balanced normal-certificate versions of the extremal principle, their space-wide validity, and the Banach-space implication from the approximate to the epsilon version.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an extremal system \{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n,\bar x\}: (i) the \varepsilon-extremal principle means that for every \varepsilon>0 there exist x_i\in\Omega_i\cap(\bar x+\varepsilon B) and x_i^*\in\widehat N_\varepsilon(x_i;\Omega_i) such that \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^*=0 and \sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i^*\|=1; (ii) the approximate extremal principle replaces these inclusions by x_i^*\in\widehat N(x_i;\Omega_i)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^* while retaining the same balance and normalization; (iii) the exact extremal principle requires x_i^*\in N(\bar x;\Omega_i) with the same balance and normalization. A version holds in X if it holds for every extremal system whose sets are locally closed around \bar x. If X is a Banach space, the approximate extremal principle implies the \varepsilon-extremal principle because \widehat N(x;\Omega)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*\subset\widehat N_\varepsilon(x;\Omega).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon and approximate principles use balanced, normalized nearby approximate-normal certificates, while the exact principle uses balanced, normalized basic normals at the reference point. Space-wide validity quantifies over locally closed extremal systems. In a Banach space, the approximate version implies the epsilon version.
assumptions_latex: \{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n,\bar x\}\text{ is an extremal system in }X
\varepsilon>0\text{ in the epsilon and approximate versions}
\Omega_i\text{ are locally closed around }\bar x\text{ when validity in }X\text{ is asserted}
X\text{ is Banach for the implication from the approximate to the epsilon principle}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^*=0,\quad\sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i^*\|=1,\quad x_i^*\in\widehat N_\varepsilon(x_i;\Omega_i),\ \widehat N(x_i;\Omega_i)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*,\text{ or }N(\bar x;\Omega_i)\text{ according to the version}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate supporting normals near boundary points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derives nearby large epsilon-normal certificates and nonzero Fréchet normals from the corresponding extremal principles, with density consequences under space-wide validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Omega\subset X be proper and closed and let \bar x\in\operatorname{bd}\Omega. If the \varepsilon-extremal principle holds for \{\Omega,\{\bar x\},\bar x\}, then for every \varepsilon>0 and every M>\varepsilon there exists x\in B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\cap\operatorname{bd}\Omega such that \widehat N_\varepsilon(x;\Omega)\setminus M\mathbb B^*\ne\varnothing. If the approximate extremal principle holds for that system, then for every \varepsilon>0 there exists x\in B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\cap\operatorname{bd}\Omega such that \widehat N(x;\Omega)\ne\{0\}. Consequently, validity of the respective principle throughout X makes the corresponding set of such points dense in \operatorname{bd}\Omega for every proper closed \Omega\subset X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near every boundary point, the epsilon-extremal principle yields an epsilon-normal whose norm exceeds any prescribed M greater than epsilon, while the approximate principle yields a nearby boundary point with a nonzero Fréchet normal. Space-wide validity makes the corresponding supporting points dense in every proper closed set's boundary.
assumptions_latex: \text{the corresponding extremal principle holds for }\{\Omega,\{\bar x\},\bar x\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x\in B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\cap\operatorname{bd}\Omega:\ \widehat N_\varepsilon(x;\Omega)\setminus M\mathbb B^*\ne\varnothing\quad\text{or}\quad\widehat N(x;\Omega)\ne\{0\},\text{ according to the assumed principle}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization of Supporting Properties by Approximate Normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between universal boundary support and two-set approximate-normal balance in a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a Banach space and let $M\geq\varepsilon\geq0$. The following properties are equivalent: (a) for every proper closed set $\Omega\subset X$, there exists $x\in\operatorname{bd}\Omega$ such that $\widehat N_\varepsilon(x;\Omega)\setminus M B^*\neq\varnothing$; (b) for arbitrary $\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X$ such that $\Omega_1-\Omega_2$ is proper and closed around $0$, there exist $x_1\in\Omega_1$ and $x_2\in\Omega_2$ satisfying $0\in\bigl(\widehat N_\varepsilon(x_1;\Omega_1)\setminus M B^*\bigr)+\widehat N_\varepsilon(x_2;\Omega_2)$. For $\varepsilon=0$, property (a) corresponds to the existence of $x\in\operatorname{bd}\Omega$ with $\widehat N(x;\Omega)\neq\{0\}$ for every proper closed $\Omega$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed 0 ≤ epsilon ≤ M, every proper closed set having a boundary point with an approximate normal outside the dual ball of radius M is equivalent to a balancing condition for approximate normals to every pair of sets whose difference is proper and closed around the origin. At epsilon zero, the support property is nontriviality of the regular normal cone at some boundary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Properties (a) and (b) are equivalent, with the stated specialization when }\varepsilon=0.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Extremal Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact limiting-normal extremal principle for a finite family in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist limiting normals \(x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\), for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), satisfying
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sum_{i=1}^m\lVert x_i^*\rVert=1.
\]
Equivalently, local extremality admits a nontrivial exact normal certificate at the common reference point. The normalization excludes the zero family and may be replaced by any equivalent positive homogeneous normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally extremal finite family of Euclidean sets that are locally closed at the common point has nonzero limiting normals there that balance exactly to zero.
assumptions_latex: The family is locally extremal at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\), not all zero, such that \(\sum_i x_i^*=0\); they may be normalized by \(\sum_i\lVert x_i^*\rVert=1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Extremal Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential encoding of nearby-point and approximate-balance extremal conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose any sequence \((\varepsilon_k)\) with \(\varepsilon_k>0\) and \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), and for each \(k\) apply the stated approximate extremal conclusion with tolerance \(\varepsilon_k\). The resulting points and normals can be denoted by \(x_{ik}\) and \(x_{ik}^*\) so that
\[
x_{ik}\to\bar x,
\qquad x_{ik}^*\in N^{\mathrm a}_{\Omega_i}(x_{ik}),
\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\lVert x_{ik}^*\rVert=1,
\qquad \left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^m x_{ik}^*\right\rVert\to0.
\]
This representation does not assert convergence of the individual dual vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying an approximate extremal conclusion along vanishing tolerances gives nearby points converging to the reference point and normalized admissible normals whose total imbalance converges to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\), and \(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\).

For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the applicable approximate extremal conclusion provides \(x_i\in\Omega_i\cap B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) and \(x_i^*\in N^{\mathrm a}_{\Omega_i}(x_i)\) satisfying \(\sum_i\lVert x_i^*\rVert=1\) and \(\lVert\sum_i x_i^*\rVert<\varepsilon\).
The symbol \(N^{\mathrm a}\) denotes the fixed normal construction in that applicable conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every sequence \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), corresponding approximants can be selected with \(x_{ik}\to\bar x\) and \(\lVert\sum_i x_{ik}^*\rVert\to0\), while \(\sum_i\lVert x_{ik}^*\rVert=1\).

notation.meaning: the fixed normal construction used by the applicable approximate extremal conclusion
positive approximation tolerances converging to zero

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\), and \(\bar x\in\bigcap_i\Omega_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is locally extremal at \(\bar x\) exactly when arbitrarily small translations can destroy its intersection inside one fixed neighborhood of \(\bar x\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Extremal Principle in Variational Analysis p. 171

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite system \(\{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\}\) is locally extremal at \(\bar x\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and vectors \(a_{ik}\in X\) such that
\[
a_{ik}\to0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),
\qquad
\bigcap_{i=1}^m(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\cap U=\varnothing
\quad\text{for every }k.
\]
Thus one fixed localization is rendered infeasible by translations whose magnitudes vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set system is locally extremal when vanishing translations make all translated sets have empty intersection in a fixed neighborhood.

children.top_down_role: Quantitative weaker separation behavior of set collections.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\), and \(\bar x\in\Omega:=\bigcap_i\Omega_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Linear subextremality holds when the distance to \(\Omega\) is locally bounded by a constant times the largest individual-set distance.

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear error-bound sense of subextremality for finite set systems.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The system \(\{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\}\) is linearly subextremal at \(\bar x\) if there exist constants \(\kappa>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
d\!\left(x,\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\right)
\le \kappa\max_{1\le i\le m}d(x,\Omega_i)
\quad\text{for every }x\in B_\delta(\bar x).
\]
This is a local metric error bound for the feasibility system; replacing the maximum by a finite sum changes only the admissible constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear subextremality is the local error bound controlling distance to the common intersection by the largest individual constraint violation.
knowledge_statements.title: Subextremality of Set Systems

children.title: Extremality–Subextremality Gap
children.top_down_role: Boundaries separating exact extremality from weaker metric behavior.

Subextremality is understood as the local linear distance error bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither property implies the other without additional hypotheses.

notation.meaning: the real line or Euclidean plane, as specified

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X=\mathbb{R}\) and \(\Omega_1=\Omega_2=X\), the subextremality inequality holds trivially, but translations cannot make the intersection locally empty, so extremality fails. Conversely, in \(X=\mathbb{R}^2\), let
\[
\Omega_1=\{(s,t):t\ge s^2\},
\qquad
\Omega_2=\{(s,t):t\le0\}.
\]
Small vertical translations separate the sets locally, so they are extremal at \((0,0)\). Along \(x_s=(s,0)\), however, \(d(x_s,\Omega_1)=O(s^2)\) while \(d(x_s,\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2)=|s|\), so no linear subextremality constant exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subextremality can hold without extremality for two full spaces, while tangentially meeting planar sets can be extremal without satisfying a linear error bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Extremality–Subextremality Gap

\qquad d(\bar x,x_0)\le\lambda,
\]
and, for every \(x\in X\setminus\{\bar x\}\),
\[
f(x)>f(\bar x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,\bar x).
\]
Equivalently, \(\bar x\) is the unique strict minimizer of \(x\mapsto f(x)+(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every approximate minimizer of a lower semicontinuous bounded-below function on a complete metric space yields a nearby strict minimizer after a small distance penalty.
knowledge_statements.title: Ekeland Variational Principle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Variational Principles and Smooth Structure of Banach Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concave-support and bump-function variants, including their converse smooth-geometry requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X$ be a Banach space, let $\mathcal A$ consist of all proper lower-semicontinuous bounded-below functions $\varphi:X	o\overline{\mathbb R}$, and fix $\varepsilon,\lambda>0$. (i) If $X$ admits a Fréchet smooth renorm, then for every $\varphi\in\mathcal A$ and $x_0$ with $\varphi(x_0)<\inf_X\varphi+\varepsilon$, there exist $ ar x$ and a concave Fréchet differentiable $s:X	o\mathbb R$ such that $\| ar x-x_0\|<\lambda$, $\varphi( ar x)<\inf_X\varphi+\varepsilon$, $\|
abla s( ar x)\|<\varepsilon/\lambda$, $\varphi( ar x)=s( ar x)$, and $\varphi(x)\geq s(x)+\|x- ar x\|^2$ for all $x$. (ii) If $X$ admits an $\mathcal S$-smooth bump function for $\mathcal S\in\{\mathcal F,\mathcal{LF},\mathcal{LC}^1\}$, then such a $ ar x$ exists together with an $\mathcal S$-smooth bump $b$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $\|
abla b( ar x)\|<\varepsilon/\lambda$, $\varphi( ar x)=b( ar x)+c$, and $\varphi(x)\geq b(x)+c$ for all $x$. Moreover, there are $\mathcal S$-smooth $s:X	o\mathbb R$ and $	heta:X	o[0,\infty)$ with $\|
abla s( ar x)\|<\varepsilon/\lambda$, $	heta(x)=0$ if and only if $x=0$, $	heta(x)\leq\|x\|^2$ for $x$ in the unit ball, $\varphi( ar x)=s( ar x)$, and $\varphi(x)\geq s(x)+	heta(x- ar x)$ for all $x$. (iii) Conversely, the concave $\mathcal F$-smooth variational principle can hold in $X$ only if $X$ admits a Fréchet smooth renorm, and the $\mathcal S$-smooth variational principle can hold only if $X$ admits a corresponding $\mathcal S$-smooth bump function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fréchet-smooth renorm or an appropriate smooth bump function yields smooth supporting perturbations at nearby strict approximate minimizers, with controlled derivative and prescribed growth. Conversely, the corresponding smooth variational principle requires the indicated smooth renorm or bump function.
assumptions_latex: \varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is proper, l.s.c., and bounded below}
\text{For (ii), }X\text{ admits an }\mathcal S\text{-smooth bump function, }\mathcal S\in\{\mathcal F,\mathcal{LF},\mathcal{LC}^1\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The corresponding smooth supporting perturbations exist at a nearby }\bar x\text{ with derivative norm }<\varepsilon/\lambda;\text{ conversely, each principle requires the stated smooth renorm or bump-function property.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke mean-value theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nonsmooth mean-value principle for a locally Lipschitz scalar function along a line segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n with x\ne y, and let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be locally Lipschitz on an open set U with [x,y]\subset U. Then there exist z\in(x,y) and v\in\partial_C f(z) such that f(y)-f(x)=v^T(y-x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is locally Lipschitz on an open set containing the segment between distinct points x and y, then at some interior point z a Clarke subgradient realizes the difference f(y) minus f(x) along y minus x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists z\in(x,y),\ \exists v\in\partial_C f(z):\ f(y)-f(x)=v^T(y-x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mean-Value Theorem for Quasidifferentiable Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-increment representation using both quasidifferential components at an intermediate point, with the theorem's alternative quantifier directions preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be quasidifferentiable on \(X\), and let \(x,x+\Delta\in X\). Then there exists \(\tau\in(0,1)\) such that either
\[\forall v\in\partial f(x+\tau\Delta)\;\exists w(v)\in\bar\partial f(x+\tau\Delta):\quad f(x+\Delta)-f(x)=\langle v+w(v),\Delta\rangle,\]
or
\[\forall w\in\bar\partial f(x+\tau\Delta)\;\exists v(w)\in\partial f(x+\tau\Delta):\quad f(x+\Delta)-f(x)=\langle v(w)+w,\Delta\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a quasidifferentiable function on an open convex set, an intermediate point exists at which one of two alternatives holds: every element of either quasidifferential component can be paired with an element of the other component so that their sum exactly represents the finite increment along the displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\tau\in(0,1)\text{ such that either }\bigl[\forall v\in\partial f(x+\tau\Delta)\;\exists w(v)\in\bar\partial f(x+\tau\Delta): f(x+\Delta)-f(x)=\langle v+w(v),\Delta\rangle\bigr]\text{ or }\bigl[\forall w\in\bar\partial f(x+\tau\Delta)\;\exists v(w)\in\partial f(x+\tau\Delta): f(x+\Delta)-f(x)=\langle v(w)+w,\Delta\rangle\bigr].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dini Mean-Value Inequality Along a Segment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds a continuous function's finite increment by extremal lower and upper Dini derivatives along the segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f$ be continuous on an open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, let $\alpha_0>0$, and suppose $x+\alpha g\in\Omega$ for every $\alpha\in[0,\alpha_0]$. Define
\[
m=\inf_{\alpha\in[0,\alpha_0]}f_D^{\downarrow}(x+\alpha g;g),\qquad M=\sup_{\alpha\in[0,\alpha_0]}f_D^{\uparrow}(x+\alpha g;g).
\]
Then
\[
m\alpha_0\le f(x+\alpha_0g)-f(x)\le M\alpha_0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The change of a continuous function along a contained segment is bounded by the segment parameter times the infimum of its lower Dini derivative and the supremum of its upper Dini derivative in the segment direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha_0\inf_{\alpha\in[0,\alpha_0]}f_D^{\downarrow}(x+\alpha g;g)\le f(x+\alpha_0g)-f(x)\le\alpha_0\sup_{\alpha\in[0,\alpha_0]}f_D^{\uparrow}(x+\alpha g;g).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[G_f(x):=\left\{p\in\mathbb R^n:\exists x_k\in D_f,\ x_k\to x,\ \nabla f(x_k)\to p\right\}.\] Then the Clarke subdifferential is generated by reachable gradients: \[\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}G_f(x).\] In finite dimensions, local Lipschitz continuity makes the nearby gradients locally bounded, and the right-hand side is a nonempty compact convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial subgradient and radial subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a real-valued function radial-directionally differentiable at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(x^0\in U\), and let \(\widehat\varphi:U\to\mathbb R\) be radial-directionally differentiable at \(x^0\). A vector \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) is a radial subgradient of \(\widehat\varphi\) at \(x^0\) if \[\widehat\varphi(x^0)+\langle r,d\rangle\leq\widehat\varphi(x^0;r)+d\widehat\varphi_{x^0}(r)\] for every \(r\) satisfying \(\widehat\varphi(x^0)\geq\widehat\varphi(x^0;r)\). The set of all radial subgradients is the radial subdifferential \(\partial_{\mathrm{rad}}\widehat\varphi(x^0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A radial subgradient satisfies the defining inequality for every direction whose radial limit does not exceed the reference value. The collection of all such vectors is the radial subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_{\mathrm{rad}}\widehat\varphi(x^0)=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\widehat\varphi(x^0)+\langle r,d\rangle\leq\widehat\varphi(x^0;r)+d\widehat\varphi_{x^0}(r)\ \forall r\text{ with }\widehat\varphi(x^0)\geq\widehat\varphi(x^0;r)\}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional, upper Dini, and Clarke directional derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definitions and comparisons of one-sided directional models, directional differentiability, and Clarke regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be real-valued and defined on a neighborhood of $x$ in a normed space $X$, and let $d\in X$. When the limit exists, the directional derivative is $f'(x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}$. The upper Dini directional derivative is $f^{(D)}(x;d):=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}$. If $f$ is Lipschitz near $x$, its Clarke generalized directional derivative is $f^\circ(x;d):=\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(y+td)-f(y)}{t}$. Under this Lipschitz hypothesis, the upper Dini and Clarke derivatives are finite and satisfy $f^{(D)}(x;d)\leq f^\circ(x;d)$. If $f'(x;d)$ exists, then $f'(x;d)=f^{(D)}(x;d)$. The function is directionally differentiable at $x$ if $f'(x;d)$ exists for every $d\in X$. It is Clarke regular at $x$ if it is directionally differentiable there and $f'(x;d)=f^\circ(x;d)$ for every $d\in X$; it is regular if it is regular at every point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary directional derivative uses a one-sided limit. The upper Dini derivative uses a limsup, while the Clarke derivative additionally permits perturbations of the base point. For locally Lipschitz functions the upper Dini derivative does not exceed the Clarke derivative. Clarke regularity means that all directional derivatives exist and agree with their Clarke counterparts.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is real-valued and defined on a neighborhood of }x
f\text{ is Lipschitz near }x\text{ for the Clarke derivative, finiteness, comparison, and regularity statements}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^{(D)}(x;d)\leq f^\circ(x;d),\qquad f'(x;d)\text{ exists}\Longrightarrow f'(x;d)=f^{(D)}(x;d),\qquad f\text{ is Clarke regular at }x\iff\forall d\in X,\ f'(x;d)\text{ exists and }f'(x;d)=f^\circ(x;d)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial subgradient and radial subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a radial-directionally differentiable real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), \(x^0\in U\), and let \(\alpha:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be radial-directionally differentiable at \(x^0\). A vector \(d\in\mathbb{R}^m\) is a radial subgradient of \(\alpha\) at \(x^0\) if, for every \(r\) satisfying \(\alpha(x^0)\geq\alpha_r(x^0)\), \[\alpha(x^0)+d^\top r\leq\alpha_r(x^0)+\mathrm d\alpha(x^0;r).\] The set of all radial subgradients is the radial subdifferential \(\partial_{\mathrm{rad}}\alpha(x^0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector d is a radial subgradient at x0 when its linear value satisfies the stated inequality for every radial comparison direction r with alpha(x0) at least alpha_r(x0). All such vectors form the radial subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_{\mathrm{rad}}\alpha(x^0)=\left\{d\in\mathbb{R}^m:\forall r,\ \alpha(x^0)\geq\alpha_r(x^0)\Rightarrow\alpha(x^0)+d^\top r\leq\alpha_r(x^0)+\mathrm d\alpha(x^0;r)\right\}.

children.top_down_role: Agreement and separation regimes for Dini versus radial information.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \(f(x)\in\mathbb R\), and \(v\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The radial derivative exists exactly when \(d_D^-f(x;v)=d_D^+f(x;v)\), and then all three values coincide.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison under the fixed-ray convention for radial differentiation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the fixed-ray quotient \(q(t):=[f(x+tv)-f(x)]/t\), one always has \[d_D^-f(x;v)\leq d_D^+f(x;v).\] The radial derivative \(f^r(x;v)\) exists in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\) if and only if \[d_D^-f(x;v)=d_D^+f(x;v).\] In that case, \[f^r(x;v)=d_D^-f(x;v)=d_D^+f(x;v).\] Equality concerns a fixed direction and does not by itself imply Hadamard directional stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radial derivative exists precisely when the lower and upper fixed-direction Dini derivatives agree; their common value is the radial derivative.

children.title: Hadamard Directional Models
children.top_down_role: Directionally stable models allowing perturbed directions.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are normed spaces, \(U\subset X\) is open, \(F:U\to Y\), \(x\in U\), and \(v\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hadamard directional differentiability requires a common quotient limit for every \(t\downarrow0\) and \(v'\to v\).

notation.meaning: Hadamard directional derivative of F at x in direction v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong one-sided directional derivative with perturbed directions.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Hadamard directionally differentiable at \(x\) in direction \(v\) if there exists \(F'_H(x;v)\in Y\) such that \[F'_H(x;v)=\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\v'\to v}}\frac{F(x+tv')-F(x)}{t}.\] Equivalently, every pair of sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(v_k\to v\), with \(x+t_kv_k\in U\), yields the same limit. If the derivative exists in direction \(v\), then for every \(\alpha>0\) it exists in direction \(\alpha v\) and satisfies \[F'_H(x;\alpha v)=\alpha F'_H(x;v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hadamard derivative is a directional difference-quotient limit stable under simultaneous small perturbations of the positive step and the direction; its values scale positively with the direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Directional Models

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Directional Chain Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chain rule for a composite of Banach-space mappings along a prescribed first- and second-order direction pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X,Y,Z$ be Banach spaces, $g:X\to Y$, and $f:Y\to Z$. Suppose $g$ is second-order directionally differentiable at $x$ in direction $h$, $f$ is Hadamard directionally differentiable at $g(x)$, and $f$ is Hadamard second-order directionally differentiable at $g(x)$ in direction $g'(x,h)$. Then $f\circ g$ is second-order directionally differentiable at $x$ in direction $h$, and for every admissible second-order direction $w$,
$$(f\circ g)''(x;h,w)=f''\bigl(g(x);g'(x,h),g''(x;h,w)\bigr).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the inner map has a second-order directional derivative and the outer map has the corresponding Hadamard first- and second-order directional derivatives, then their composite has a second-order directional derivative given by composing those directional data.
assumptions_latex: $g:X\to Y$ is second-order directionally differentiable at $x$ in direction $h$.
$f:Y\to Z$ is Hadamard directionally differentiable at $g(x)$.
$f$ is Hadamard second-order directionally differentiable at $g(x)$ in direction $g'(x,h)$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (f\circ g)''(x;h,w)=f''\bigl(g(x);g'(x,h),g''(x;h,w)\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Bouligand derivative of \(F\) at \(x\) is the positively homogeneous set-valued mapping \[DF(x)(h):=\{k\in Y:(h,k)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(x,F(x))\}.\] Equivalently, \(k\in DF(x)(h)\) if and only if there are \(t_j\downarrow0\), \(h_j\to h\), and \(k_j\to k\) such that \[F(x+t_jh_j)=F(x)+t_jk_j.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bouligand derivative collects output velocities paired with an input velocity in the tangent cone to the mapping's graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Bouligand semidifferentiable at \(x\) in direction \(h\) if a vector \(F'_B(x;h)\in Y\) exists such that \[F'_B(x;h)=\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}\frac{F(x+th')-F(x)}{t}.\] Equivalently, \[F(x+th')=F(x)+tF'_B(x;h)+r(t,h'),\qquad \frac{\|r(t,h')\|}{t}\to0\] as \(t\downarrow0\) and \(h'\to h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand semidifferentiability in a specified direction requires all nearby-direction difference quotients to converge to one first-order vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the Clarke generalized directional model is \[f^{\circ}(\bar x;d):=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\ t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}.\] It is finite, positively homogeneous, and subadditive in \(d\). Defining \(\partial_C f(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,d\rangle\leq f^{\circ}(\bar x;d)\text{ for all }d\in\mathbb{R}^n\}\), one has \[f^{\circ}(\bar x;d)=\max_{v\in\partial_C f(\bar x)}\langle v,d\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke model convexifies nearby upper directional quotients and equals the support function of the Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Generalized Directional Models

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sublinearity and ordering of generalized directional derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison theorem for a function with a local Lipschitz constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the real-valued function \(f\) has Lipschitz constant \(K\) around \(x\in\mathbf E\), then \(f^\circ(x;\cdot)\) and \(f^\diamond(x;\cdot)\) are sublinear and, for every \(h\in\mathbf E\), \[f^-(x;h)\le f^\diamond(x;h)\le f^\circ(x;h)\le K\|h\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is locally K-Lipschitz around x, its Clarke and Michel–Penot directional derivatives are sublinear. At every direction, the lower Dini derivative is bounded above by the Michel–Penot derivative, which is bounded above by the Clarke derivative and then by K times the direction norm.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has Lipschitz constant \(K\) in a neighborhood of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^\circ(x;\cdot)\) and \(f^\diamond(x;\cdot)\) are sublinear, and \(f^-(x;h)\le f^\diamond(x;h)\le f^\circ(x;h)\le K\|h\|\) for all \(h\in\mathbf E\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The regular lower subderivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is the extended-real quantity \[d f(\bar x)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\ w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] Equivalently, its epigraph is the outer limit of the epigraphs of the first-order difference quotients \(w\mapsto [f(\bar x+t w)-f(\bar x)]/t\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Thus perturbations of both step size and direction are included in the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular lower subderivative is the lower limit of first-order quotients under simultaneous perturbation of step and direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity, Positive Homogeneity, and Support Inequality of the Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded structural theorem for directional derivatives of convex extended-real-valued functions; it does not assert a subgradient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex and let \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). For \(p\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \[f'(x;p):=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha p)-f(x)}{\alpha},\] where the limit exists, possibly in \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). Then \(p\mapsto f'(x;p)\) is convex and satisfies \[f'(x;\tau p)=\tau f'(x;p)\qquad\forall p\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \forall\tau>0.\] Moreover, \[f(y)\geq f(x)+f'(x;y-x)\qquad\forall y\in\operatorname{dom}f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an ambient-interior domain point of a convex extended-real-valued function, the directional derivative is a convex function of the direction and is positively homogeneous under every positive scaling. It also supplies a global lower bound for the function along the displacement to any other domain point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\mapsto f'(x;p)\text{ is convex},\quad f'(x;\tau p)=\tau f'(x;p)\ \forall p\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \forall\tau>0,\quad f(y)\geq f(x)+f'(x;y-x)\ \forall y\in\operatorname{dom}f.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity, Positive Homogeneity, and Global Support of the Convex Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded structural result at an interior point of the effective domain; no subgradient representation is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex and let \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). For every \(p\in\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
f'(x;p):=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha p)-f(x)}{\alpha},
\]
where the limit exists, possibly as an extended-real number. Then \(p\mapsto f'(x;p)\) is convex and
\[
f'(x;\tau p)=\tau f'(x;p)\qquad\text{for all }p\in\mathbb R^n\text{ and }\tau>0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+f'(x;y-x)\qquad\text{for every }y\in\operatorname{dom}f.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior point of the effective domain of a convex function, the directional derivative is a convex, positively homogeneous function of the direction and gives a global lower support inequality for every point in the effective domain.
assumptions_latex: \forall p\in\mathbb R^n,\ f'(x;p)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha p)-f(x)}{\alpha}\text{ exists in }\overline{\mathbb R}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\mapsto f'(x;p)\text{ is convex},\quad \forall p\in\mathbb R^n,\ \forall\tau>0,\ f'(x;\tau p)=\tau f'(x;p),\quad \forall y\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ f(y)\ge f(x)+f'(x;y-x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitz continuity upgrades directional differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An implication from fixed-direction differentiability to Hadamard directional differentiability, with preservation of the local Lipschitz modulus in the direction variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose $g:X\to Y$ is directionally differentiable at $x$ and is Lipschitz continuous with modulus $c$ on a neighborhood of $x$. Then $g$ is Hadamard directionally differentiable at $x$, and $$\|g'(x,h_1)-g'(x,h_2)\|\le c\|h_1-h_2\|\qquad\forall h_1,h_2\in X.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a mapping is directionally differentiable at x and locally Lipschitz near x with modulus c, it is Hadamard directionally differentiable there, and its directional derivative is Lipschitz in the direction variable with the same modulus.
assumptions_latex: g:X\to Y\text{ is directionally differentiable at }x
\|g(u)-g(v)\|\le c\|u-v\|\text{ for all }u,v\text{ in a neighborhood of }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is Hadamard directionally differentiable at }x,\qquad\|g'(x,h_1)-g'(x,h_2)\|\le c\|h_1-h_2\|\quad\forall h_1,h_2\in X.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The symbols \(f_-^{\downarrow}\), \(f_+^{\downarrow}\), and \(T^i\) retain the source's lower and upper epigraphical derivative and inner-tangent notation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Endpoint increase forces a positive directional derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrapositive endpoint-growth form of a directional monotonicity principle for extended-real-valued functions on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper, let x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f and x_1\in\mathcal H, and suppose [x_0,x_1)\subset\operatorname{dom}f, f(x_0)<f(x_1), and f|_{(x_0,x_1]} is lower semicontinuous. If f'(x;x_1-x_0) exists for every x\in[x_0,x_1), then there exists z\in[x_0,x_1) such that f'(z;x_1-x_0)>0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let f be a proper extended-real-valued function on a Hilbert space. If the half-open segment from x0 to x1 lies in its domain, f is lower semicontinuous on the segment excluding x0, its value strictly increases from x0 to x1, and every directional derivative toward x1 exists along the half-open segment, then one of those derivatives is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists z\in[x_0,x_1)\text{ such that }f'(z;x_1-x_0)>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-sided derivatives and subgradients of a convex function on the line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper extended-real-valued convex functions on \(\mathbb R\); derivative comparisons are asserted on the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then
\[
f'_{-}(x)\le f'_{+}(x),\qquad
\partial f(x)=[f'_{-}(x),f'_{+}(x)]\cap\mathbb R.
\]
If \(x<y\), then
\[
f'_{+}(x)\le f'_{-}(y).
\]
Consequently, both \(f'_{-}\) and \(f'_{+}\) are increasing on \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function on the real line, the left derivative does not exceed the right derivative, and the subdifferential is the interval between them, restricted to finite real values. At distinct domain points x<y, the right derivative at x does not exceed the left derivative at y; hence both one-sided derivative functions are increasing on the domain.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'_{-}(x)\le f'_{+}(x),\quad \partial f(x)=[f'_{-}(x),f'_{+}(x)]\cap\mathbb R,\quad x<y\implies f'_{+}(x)\le f'_{-}(y),\quad f'_{-},f'_{+}\text{ are increasing on }\operatorname{dom}f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-dimensional one-sided derivative criterion for convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper extended-real-valued functions whose effective domain is an interval in the real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper and let I=\operatorname{dom}f be an interval. Suppose f|_I is lower semicontinuous, the one-sided derivatives f'_+(x) and f'_-(x) exist for every x\in I, and f'_+(x)\le f'_-(y) whenever x,y\in I and x<y. Then f is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let f be a proper extended-real-valued function on the real line whose domain is an interval. If f is lower semicontinuous on its domain, both one-sided derivatives exist at every domain point, and every right derivative at an earlier point is at most every left derivative at a later point, then f is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-point directional-derivative criterion for convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper extended-real-valued functions on a Hilbert space with convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper. Suppose \operatorname{dom}f is convex, f|_{\operatorname{dom}f} is lower semicontinuous, and for every x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f the directional derivatives f'(x;y-x) and f'(y;x-y) exist and satisfy f'(x;y-x)\le -f'(y;x-y). Then f is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-real-valued function is convex if its domain is convex, its restriction to that domain is lower semicontinuous, and at every ordered pair of domain points the directional derivative from the first toward the second is at most the negative of the reverse directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structure of the directional derivative of a proper convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the extended-real existence result, comparison inequalities, sublinearity, domain formula, and the stronger core-domain conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(y\in\mathcal H\). Then \(f'(x;y)\) exists in \([-\infty,+\infty]\) and \[f'(x;y)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R_{++}}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)-f(x)}{\alpha}.\] Moreover, \(f'(x;y-x)+f(x)\le f(y)\); if \(y\in\operatorname{dom}f\), then \(f'(x;y-x)\le-f'(y;x-y)\). The function \(f'(x;\cdot)\) is sublinear with \(f'(x;0)=0\), is proper and convex, and satisfies \[\operatorname{dom}f'(x;\cdot)=\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{dom}f-x).\] If \(x\in\operatorname{core}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), then \(f'(x;\cdot)\) is real-valued and sublinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every domain point of a proper convex function, every fixed-direction derivative exists as an extended-real limit and equals the infimum of all positive secant slopes. It gives a lower affine estimate toward any point, obeys an opposite-direction comparison between two domain points, and forms a proper convex sublinear function of the direction whose domain is the cone generated by the translated function domain. At a core-domain point it is finite in every direction.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
y\in\operatorname{dom}f\text{ for the two-point directional inequality}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{gathered}f'(x;y)=\inf_{\alpha>0}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)-f(x)}{\alpha},\qquad f'(x;y-x)+f(x)\le f(y),\\ y\in\operatorname{dom}f\Rightarrow f'(x;y-x)\le-f'(y;x-y),\\ f'(x;\cdot)\text{ is proper, convex, and sublinear},\quad f'(x;0)=0,\\ \operatorname{dom}f'(x;\cdot)=\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{dom}f-x),\\ x\in\operatorname{core}(\operatorname{dom}f)\Rightarrow f'(x;\cdot)\text{ is real-valued}.\end{gathered}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\in X\) if, for every \(d\in X\), there exists an element \(F'(\bar x;d)\in Y\) such that \[F'(\bar x;d)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{F(\bar x+t d)-F(\bar x)}{t}.\] The direction \(d\) remains fixed in this limit. The resulting map \(d\mapsto F'(\bar x;d)\) is positively homogeneous whenever it is defined in all directions, but linearity is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional differentiability requires a one-sided derivative along every fixed direction, without requiring the derivative map to be linear.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite One-Sided Directional Derivative in a Fixed Direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition requiring a fixed nonzero direction and a finite right-hand difference-quotient limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(p\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\). The function \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) in direction \(p\) if the finite limit \[f'(x;p)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha p)-f(x)}{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}\] exists. This value is the directional derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) in direction \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional differentiability at a domain point along a fixed nonzero direction means that the forward difference quotient has a finite real limit as the positive step tends to zero. That limit is the directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is differentiable at }x\text{ in direction }p\iff \exists f'(x;p)\in\mathbb{R}:\ f'(x;p)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha p)-f(x)}{\alpha}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative of a finite max-function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The derivative is determined only by component functions active at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\bar x\in\operatorname{int}C$, let the continuous functions $g_0,\ldots,g_m:C\to\mathbf R$ be differentiable at $\bar x$, define $g(x)=\max_{0\le i\le m}g_i(x)$ and $K=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=g(\bar x)\}$. Then, for every $d\in\mathbf E$, $$g'(\bar x;d)=\max_{i\in K}\langle\nabla g_i(\bar x),d\rangle.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior point, the directional derivative of a finite maximum of differentiable functions is the maximum of the active component directional derivatives.
assumptions_latex: g_i:C\to\mathbf R\text{ is continuous on }C\text{ and differentiable at }\bar x\quad(i=0,\ldots,m)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall d\in\mathbf E,\qquad g'(\bar x;d)=\max_{i\in K}\langle\nabla g_i(\bar x),d\rangle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the directional derivative along a fixed nonzero direction and records the negative-derivative descent implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(v\ne0\), whenever the limit exists, the directional derivative is \[f'(x;v):=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha v)-f(x)}{\alpha}.\] If \(f'(x;v)<0\), then \(v\) is a descent direction at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative is the one-sided rate of change along a fixed nonzero direction. If it is negative, the direction gives descent for sufficiently small positive steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x;v)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha v)-f(x)}{\alpha},\qquad f'(x;v)<0\Rightarrow v\text{ is a descent direction at }x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative and one-sided derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-direction derivatives of a proper extended-real-valued function, conditioned on existence of the indicated extended-real limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(y\in\mathcal H\). Provided the limit exists in \([ -\infty,+\infty]\), \[f'(x;y)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)-f(x)}{\alpha}.\] If \(\mathcal H=\mathbb R\), then, whenever the respective limits exist, \[f'_+(x)=f'(x;1)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha)-f(x)}{\alpha}\] and \[f'_-(x)=-f'(x;-1)=\lim_{\alpha\uparrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha)-f(x)}{\alpha}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative is the right-hand difference-quotient limit along a fixed direction, when that limit exists in the extended reals. In one dimension, directions 1 and −1 give the right and left derivatives with the stated sign convention.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each derivative is defined only when its indicated extended-real limit exists}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x;y)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)-f(x)}{\alpha},\qquad \mathcal H=\mathbb R\Rightarrow\left\{\begin{aligned}f'_+(x)&=f'(x;1),\\f'_-(x)&=-f'(x;-1).\end{aligned}\right.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F'_H(\bar x;d)\) exists for every \(d\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hadamard directional differentiability, allowing simultaneous perturbation of direction and step.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Hadamard directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\in X\) if, for every \(d\in X\), there exists \(F'_H(\bar x;d)\in Y\) such that \[F'_H(\bar x;d)=\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\ d'\to d}}\frac{F(\bar x+t d')-F(\bar x)}{t}.\] Equivalently, the displayed quotient converges to the same value along every pair of sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(d_k\to d\). This stability under directional perturbations distinguishes it from ordinary directional differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hadamard differentiability requires directional quotients to converge even when the direction varies toward the target direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Differentiability

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient characterizations of strict Hadamard differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between strict Hadamard differentiability and singleton limiting-subgradient behavior under local Lipschitz continuity in an Asplund space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an Asplund space, let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be finite at \(\bar x\), and let \(\xi\in X^*\). The following are equivalent: (a) \(\varphi\) is Lipschitz continuous around \(\bar x\), and for every sequence \(x_k\to\bar x\) and every choice \(x_k^*\in\widehat\partial\varphi(x_k)\), one has \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}\xi\); (b) \(\varphi\) is Lipschitz continuous around \(\bar x\) and \(\partial\varphi(\bar x)=\{\xi\}\); and (c) \(\varphi\) is strictly Hadamard differentiable at \(\bar x\) with \(\nabla\varphi(\bar x)=\xi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function finite at a reference point in an Asplund space, strict Hadamard differentiability with derivative ξ is equivalent to local Lipschitz continuity together with either weak-star convergence of every nearby Fréchet-subgradient selection to ξ or a singleton limiting subdifferential at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [(\(\varphi\) is locally Lipschitz and every \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(x_k^*\in\widehat\partial\varphi(x_k)\) satisfies \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}\xi\))]\(\Longleftrightarrow\)[\(\varphi\) is locally Lipschitz and \(\partial\varphi(\bar x)=\{\xi\}\)]\(\Longleftrightarrow\)[\(\varphi\) is strictly Hadamard differentiable at \(\bar x\) with \(\nabla\varphi(\bar x)=\xi\)].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued functions defined near a point in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ if there exists a vector $
abla f(x)$ such that $$f(x+v)=f(x)+\langle
abla f(x),vangle+o(v),\qquad  rac{o(v)}{\|v\|}	o0\quad(\|v\|	o0).$$ It is then directionally differentiable with the continuous linear derivative $f'(x;g)=\langle
abla f(x),gangle$. In this finite-dimensional setting, this is equivalent to Hadamard differentiability with a linear derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fréchet differentiability requires one linear approximation whose error is uniformly negligible relative to the increment norm. It yields a continuous linear directional derivative and is equivalent here to linear Hadamard differentiability.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is real-valued and defined on a neighborhood of }x\in\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x;g)=\langle\nabla f(x),g\rangle\ \forall g,\quad f\text{ is linearly Hadamard differentiable at }x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Derivative and First Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided directional differentiation for a mapping between linear spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in\mathcal U\) and \(h\in U\), if the admissible right-hand limit \[\delta F(u,h):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{F(u+th)-F(u)}{t}\] exists in \(V\), it is the directional derivative of \(F\) at \(u\) in direction \(h\). If it exists for every \(h\in U\), then \(h\mapsto\delta F(u,h)\) is the first variation of \(F\) at \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative is the V-valued right-hand limit of the difference quotient along domain-admissible increments. If it exists in every direction, the resulting mapping is the first variation.
assumptions_latex: u+th\in\mathcal U\text{ for the positive parameters used in the limit}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta F(u,h)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{F(u+th)-F(u)}{t};\quad (\forall h\in U)\Rightarrow[h\mapsto\delta F(u,h)\text{ is the first variation at }u].

children.title: Bouligand Differentiability
children.top_down_role: Positively homogeneous first-order approximation regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\bar x+h)=F(\bar x)+B(h)+o(\lVert h\rVert)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Bouligand differentiability via a uniform positively homogeneous first-order approximation.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Bouligand-Differentiable Functions p. 150

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(\bar x\) if there exists a continuous positively homogeneous mapping \(B:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \[F(\bar x+h)=F(\bar x)+B(h)+r(h),\qquad \lim_{h\to0,\,h\neq0}\frac{\lVert r(h)\rVert}{\lVert h\rVert}=0.\] The map \(B\) is the Bouligand derivative. It need not be linear; when directional derivatives exist, the approximation forces \(B(d)=F'(\bar x;d)\) for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand differentiability provides a uniform first-order approximation by a continuous positively homogeneous, possibly nonlinear, derivative map.
knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand Differentiability

children.top_down_role: Agreement between ordinary and convexified directional behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(\bar x;d)=f^{\circ}(\bar x;d)\) for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar x\) if, for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the ordinary one-sided directional derivative \[f'(\bar x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+td)-f(\bar x)}{t}\] exists and satisfies \[f'(\bar x;d)=f^{\circ}(\bar x;d).\] Thus the directional behavior observed at the fixed base point agrees in every direction with the convexified upper behavior obtained from nearby base points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz function is Clarke regular when every ordinary directional derivative equals its Clarke generalized directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke-Regular Functions

children.title: Calmness
children.top_down_role: One-sided local growth control relative to a reference point.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert F(x)-F(\bar x)\rVert\leq\kappa\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\) locally at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued pointwise calmness; set-valued calmness requires a different graph-based formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is calm at \(\bar x\in X\) if there exist constants \(\kappa\geq0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that \[\lVert F(x)-F(\bar x)\rVert\leq\kappa\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\qquad\text{whenever }\lVert x-\bar x\rVert<\delta.\] Unlike local Lipschitz continuity, this estimate compares nearby values only with the fixed reference value \(F(\bar x)\), not with each other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calmness bounds change from one fixed base value linearly in the distance from the base point.
knowledge_statements.title: Calmness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed estimate is a standard single-valued pointwise calmness convention, and the definition content kind fits the leaf, but no source establishes that this is the convention intended by the local taxonomy rather than a set-valued graph formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Calmness of a set-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided local Lipschitz control at a reference graph point, including the upper-Lipschitz specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping \Gamma:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m is calm at (x^0,y^0)\in\operatorname{gph}\Gamma if there exist neighborhoods U of x^0 and V of y^0 and a finite L such that \[\Gamma(x)\cap V\subseteq\Gamma(x^0)+L\|x-x^0\|\mathbb{B}\qquad\forall x\in U.\] If V=\mathbb{R}^m, this reduces to the upper Lipschitz property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping is calm at a graph point if, locally in the argument and value, every nearby image lies within a distance proportional to the argument displacement from the reference image. Taking the value neighborhood to be the whole codomain gives the upper Lipschitz property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma(x)\cap V\subseteq\Gamma(x^0)+L\|x-x^0\|\mathbb{B}\quad\forall x\in U.

children.title: Directional Lipschitz Behavior
children.top_down_role: Lipschitz growth restricted to selected directional regions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is Lipschitz on a sufficiently small conical neighborhood of direction \(d\) from \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: truncated conical neighborhood based at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise Lipschitz behavior on a truncated cone around one nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon,[39mdelta>0\), set \[C(\bar x,d;\varepsilon,\delta):=\{\bar x+t w:0\leq t<\delta,\ \lVert w-d\rVert<\varepsilon\}.\] The function \(f\) has directional Lipschitz behavior at \(\bar x\) along \(d\) if there exist \(L,[39mepsilon,\delta>0\) such that \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\lVert x-y\rVert\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C(\bar x,d;\varepsilon,\delta).\] This is a pairwise estimate restricted to a directional neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional Lipschitz behavior is ordinary pairwise Lipschitz continuity restricted to a small cone around a chosen direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Lipschitz Behavior

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied for this particular cone-based meaning of directional Lipschitz behavior, so its neighborhood geometry and pairwise estimate cannot be validated against the intended terminology. The statement also contains stray `[39m` control-text fragments. A sourced formulation is required before a reliable replacement can be made.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hypertangent characterization of directional Lipschitzness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued functions finite at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), let \(f(x)<+\infty\), and let \(v\in X\). Then
\[
f\text{ is directionally Lipschitz at }x\text{ with respect to }v
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists\beta\in\mathbb R\text{ such that }(v,\beta)\text{ is hypertangent to }\operatorname{epi}f\text{ at }(x,f(x)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function finite at x is directionally Lipschitz there with respect to v exactly when the epigraph has a hypertangent of the form (v,beta) for some real beta at (x,f(x)).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is directionally Lipschitz at }x\text{ with respect to }v\iff\exists\beta\in\mathbb R:\ (v,\beta)\text{ is hypertangent to }\operatorname{epi}f\text{ at }(x,f(x))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Lipschitzness for an extended-real-valued function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional growth regularity at a point where the function is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(v\in X\), define
\[
f^+(x;v):=\limsup_{\substack{(y,\alpha)\downarrow_f x,\ w\to v\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(y+tw)-\alpha}{t}.
\]
Assuming \(f(x)\) is finite, \(f\) is directionally Lipschitz at \(x\) with respect to \(v\) when \(f^+(x;v)\neq+\infty\). It is directionally Lipschitz at \(x\) when this holds for at least one \(v\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite point x, f is directionally Lipschitz with respect to v when its epigraphically perturbed upper directional growth is not plus infinity. Directional Lipschitzness at x requires at least one such direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is directionally Lipschitz at }x\iff\exists v\in X:\ f^+(x;v)\neq+\infty
