children.title: Calmness–Directional Lipschitz Gap
children.top_down_role: Regimes where pointwise growth control fails to extend directionally.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is calm at \(0\) but is not directionally Lipschitz there along \(d=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation of pointwise calmness from pairwise directional Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \(|f(x)-f(0)|\leq |x|^2\), so on \(|x|<1\) one has \(|f(x)-f(0)|\leq|x|\); hence \(f\) is calm at \(0\). For \(x\neq0\), \[f'(x)=2x\sin(x^{-2})-2x^{-1}\cos(x^{-2}),\] which is unbounded on every interval \((0,\delta)\). Consequently, \(f\) cannot be Lipschitz on any truncated cone around the positive direction \(d=1\). Thus calmness does not imply directional Lipschitz behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oscillatory function x-squared times sine of inverse x-squared is calm at zero but not Lipschitz on any positive directional neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Calmness–Directional Lipschitz Gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example plausibly separates calmness from pairwise Lipschitz behavior on positive directional neighborhoods, and the counterexample content kind fits the gap leaf. However, it has no cited source and the statement includes verification/proof text, which must be removed in a future sourced candidate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Lipschitzness from the effective directional domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization under local epigraph closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be finite-dimensional and suppose \operatorname{epi}f is locally closed near (x,f(x)). Then D_f(x)=\operatorname{int}\{v:f^{\circ}(x;v)<\infty\}. Consequently, f is directionally Lipschitz at x if and only if \{v:f^{\circ}(x;v)<\infty\} has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, if the epigraph of f is locally closed near (x,f(x)), then the directional-Lipschitz domain is the interior of the directions where the generalized directional derivative is finite. Thus f is directionally Lipschitz at x exactly when that set has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_f(x)=\operatorname{int}\{v:f^{\circ}(x;v)<\infty\},\qquad f\text{ is directionally Lipschitz at }x\iff\operatorname{int}\{v:f^{\circ}(x;v)<\infty\}\neq\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Effective domain and continuity of the generalized directional derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the directional-Lipschitz domain at a point where that domain is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be finite at x and suppose D_f(x)\neq\varnothing. Then D_f(x)=\operatorname{int}\{v:f^{\circ}(x;v)<\infty\}. Moreover, v\mapsto f^{\circ}(x;v) is continuous at every v\in D_f(x), and f^{\circ}(x;v)=f^{+}(x;v) there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is finite at x and its directional-Lipschitz domain D_f(x) is nonempty, then D_f(x) is the interior of the set of directions where the generalized directional derivative is finite. On this domain the generalized directional derivative is continuous and agrees with the upper directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_f(x)=\operatorname{int}\{v:f^{\circ}(x;v)<\infty\},\quad f^{\circ}(x;\cdot)\text{ is continuous on }D_f(x),\quad f^{\circ}(x;v)=f^{+}(x;v)\ \forall v\in D_f(x).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A descent direction yields strict objective decrease for every sufficiently small positive step, while remaining in the effective domain.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{|\partial f|}(x)=\liminf_{y\to x,\,f(y)\to f(x)}|\partial f|(y)\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-semicontinuous relaxation of the local slope along graph-convergent points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Given the local slope \(|\partial f|\), its limiting slope at \(x\) is \(\overline{|\partial f|}(x):=\liminf_{y\to x,\,f(y)\to f(x)}|\partial f|(y)\). Equivalently, the limit inferior is taken over all sequences \(y_n\to x\) satisfying \(f(y_n)\to f(x)\); the constant sequence is permitted.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). The asymptotic, or strict outer, slope at \(x\) is \(\overline{|\partial f|}^{>}(x):=\liminf_{y\to x,\,f(x)<f(y)\to f(x)}|\partial f|(y)\), with value \(+\infty\) if no such approaching points exist. Thus only points lying strictly above the reference level participate in the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The asymptotic slope relaxes local slopes along nearby points whose values decrease to the reference value strictly from above.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the preceding definitions, \(\overline{|\partial f|}(x)\le \overline{|\partial f|}^{>}(x)\) because the asymptotic relaxation uses a smaller class of approaching points. Equality need not hold. For \(f(t)=|t|\) on \(\mathbb R\) at \(x=0\), one has \(|\partial f|(0)=0\) and \(|\partial f|(t)=1\) for \(t\ne0\). Consequently, \(\overline{|\partial f|}(0)=0\), whereas \(\overline{|\partial f|}^{>}(0)=1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Derivative of a Proper Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided directional derivative at a domain point, including its extended-real existence and infimum formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper and convex, \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Define \(f'(x;d)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha d)-f(x)}{\alpha}\). The difference quotient is nonincreasing as \(\alpha\downarrow0\), so this limit exists in \([ -\infty,\infty]\), and \(f'(x;d)=\inf_{\alpha>0}\frac{f(x+\alpha d)-f(x)}{\alpha}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function, the one-sided directional derivative at any domain point is the limit of the forward difference quotient. Convexity makes these quotients decrease as the step tends to zero, so the extended-real limit exists and equals their infimum over positive steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x;d)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha d)-f(x)}{\alpha}=\inf_{\alpha>0}\frac{f(x+\alpha d)-f(x)}{\alpha}\in[-\infty,\infty].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Derivative as the Support Function of the Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex directional calculus at an interior point of the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex and let $x_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)$. Define $f'(x_0;p):=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x_0+\alpha p)-f(x_0)}{\alpha}$. Then $p\mapsto f'(x_0;p)$ is finite and convex on $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\partial_2f'(x_0;0)=\partial f(x_0)$, and $f'(x_0;p)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x_0)}\langle g,p\rangle$ for every $p\in\mathbb{R}^n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior point of the domain of a proper convex function, the directional derivative is a finite convex function of the direction. Its subdifferential at the zero direction equals the original subdifferential, and each directional derivative is the support value of that subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x_0;\cdot)\text{ is finite and convex},\quad \partial_2f'(x_0;0)=\partial f(x_0),\quad f'(x_0;p)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x_0)}\langle g,p\rangle\quad\forall p\in\mathbb{R}^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Directional Derivative and Basic Properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the definition with the independent monotonicity, infimum representation, convexity, and finiteness boundaries stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper convex f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty], x\in\operatorname{dom}f, and d\in\mathbb{R}^n, define f'(x;d)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha d)-f(x)}{\alpha}. The difference quotient decreases as \alpha\downarrow0, so the extended-real limit exists and f'(x;d)=\inf_{\alpha>0}\frac{f(x+\alpha d)-f(x)}{\alpha}. For fixed x, f'(x;\cdot) is convex. If x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f), then f'(x;d)\in\mathbb{R} for every d\in\mathbb{R}^n and -f'(x;-d)\leq f'(x;d). More generally, if x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f), then f'(x;d) is real for every d parallel to \operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function's directional derivative is the decreasing-limit, or equivalently the infimum, of its forward difference quotients. It is convex as a function of direction. It is finite in every direction at an interior point, and at a relative-interior point it is finite along the subspace parallel to the affine hull of the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x;d)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha d)-f(x)}{\alpha}=\inf_{\alpha>0}\frac{f(x+\alpha d)-f(x)}{\alpha},\quad f'(x;\cdot)\text{ is convex, with the stated interior and relative-interior finiteness properties}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differentiation of an Integral of Parametric Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity, continuity, and derivative interchange for a nonnegative-measure integral functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:X\times\Omega\to\mathbb R\) be jointly continuous, suppose \(g(\cdot,\omega)\) is convex for every \(\omega\in\Omega\), let \(\mu\in C(\Omega)^*\) be a nonnegative measure, and define \(\gamma(x)=\int_\Omega g(x,\omega)\,d\mu(\omega)\). Then \(\gamma\) is convex and continuous, and for all \(x,h\in X\), \(\gamma'(x;h)=\int_\Omega g_\omega'(x;h)\,d\mu(\omega)\). If \(g(\cdot,\omega)\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(x\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(\omega\), then \(\gamma\) is Hadamard differentiable at \(x\) and \(D\gamma(x)h=\int_\Omega D_xg(x,\omega)h\,d\mu(\omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative-measure integral of jointly continuous convex sections is convex and continuous, and its directional derivative is the integral of the sectional directional derivatives. Almost-everywhere Gâteaux differentiability of the sections yields Hadamard differentiability of the integral with the corresponding derivative formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma\text{ is convex and continuous},\quad \gamma'(x;h)=\int_\Omega g_\omega'(x;h)\,d\mu;\text{ under a.e. Gâteaux differentiability, }D\gamma(x)h=\int_\Omega D_xg(x,\omega)h\,d\mu.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support-Function Representation of the Convex Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the general closed-hull representation from the direct representation at relative-interior points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty] be proper and convex. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Convex Lipschitz Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the stated minimizer, generalized-subgradient, and directional-derivative equivalences. The closing announcement of a subsequent strong-minimum theorem and the unsupported aside about convex functions being Lipschitz are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }f:X\to\mathbb{R}\text{ be convex and Lipschitz. Then }x^*\text{ is a local minimizer of }f\Longleftrightarrow 0\in\partial f(x^*)\Longleftrightarrow f^o(x^*;d)\geq 0\ \forall d\in X.\text{ Moreover, }f^o(x;d)=f'(x;d)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex Lipschitz function, x* is a local minimizer exactly when zero belongs to its generalized subdifferential, equivalently when its generalized directional derivative is nonnegative in every direction. In this regime the generalized directional derivative equals the ordinary one-sided directional derivative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential representation by directional derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional-derivative characterization of convex subgradients, with boundedness at interior domain points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,\infty] be convex and x\in\operatorname{dom}f. Then \partial f(x)=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^m:f'(x;d)\ge\xi^Td\ \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^m\}. If x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f), then f'(x;d) is finite for every d, and every \xi\in\partial f(x) satisfies \|\xi\|_2=\sup_{\|d\|_2\le1}\xi^Td\le\sup_{\|d\|_2\le1}f'(x;d)<\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function, a vector is a subgradient exactly when its inner product with every direction does not exceed the corresponding directional derivative. At an interior domain point, this also gives a finite norm bound for every subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^m:f'(x;d)\ge\xi^Td\ \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^m\},\qquad \|\xi\|_2\le\sup_{\|d\|_2\le1}f'(x;d)<\infty\text{ at interior points}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Properties and Support Representation of the Clarke Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sublinearity, continuity, support-function representation, and joint upper semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz on the open set \(\Omega\). For every \(x\in\Omega\), the function \(d\mapsto g^\circ(x;d)\) is Lipschitz continuous, positively homogeneous, and sublinear; in particular,
\[
g^\circ(x;d+d')\le g^\circ(x;d)+g^\circ(x;d')\qquad(d,d'\in\mathbb{R}^n).
\]
For every \((x,d)\in\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
g^\circ(x;d)=\max_{\xi\in\partial g(x)}\xi^Td.
\]
Furthermore, \((x,d)\mapsto g^\circ(x;d)\) is upper semicontinuous on \(\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz function, the Clarke generalized directional derivative is a Lipschitz, positively homogeneous, sublinear function of the direction. It is the support function of the Clarke subdifferential and is jointly upper semicontinuous in the base point and direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g^\circ(x;\cdot)\text{ is Lipschitz, positively homogeneous, and sublinear},\quad g^\circ(x;d)=\max_{\xi\in\partial g(x)}\xi^Td,\quad g^\circ\text{ is upper semicontinuous in }(x,d)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structure and Representations of Clarke Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes Clarke and Clarke horizon subdifferentials through the regularized subderivative, recession geometry, and limiting subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be locally lower semicontinuous and finite at \(\bar x\). Then \(\bar\partial f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, \(\bar\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) is a closed convex cone, and
\[
\bar\partial f(\bar x)=\{v\mid \langle v,w\rangle\leq \widehat d f(\bar x)(w)\ \forall w\in\mathbb R^n\},
\]
\[
\bar\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{v\mid \langle v,w\rangle\leq0\ \forall w\in\operatorname{dom}\widehat d f(\bar x)\}.
\]
If \(\bar\partial f(\bar x)\neq\varnothing\), equivalently \(\partial f(\bar x)\neq\varnothing\), then
\[
\bar\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=(\bar\partial f(\bar x))^\infty,
\qquad \widehat d f(\bar x)(w)=\sup_{v\in\bar\partial f(\bar x)}\langle v,w\rangle\quad\forall w.
\]
If \(\bar\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) is pointed—equivalently, if \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) is pointed—then
\[
\bar\partial f(\bar x)=\operatorname{con}\partial f(\bar x)+\operatorname{con}\partial^\infty f(\bar x),
\qquad \bar\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\operatorname{con}\partial^\infty f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally lower-semicontinuous function finite at the reference point, the Clarke subdifferential is closed and convex and is characterized by inequalities against the regularized subderivative; the Clarke horizon subdifferential is a closed convex cone characterized by the domain of that subderivative. Under nonemptiness it is the recession cone of the Clarke subdifferential and the regularized subderivative is its support function. Under the stated pointedness condition, both Clarke objects admit convex-hull formulas in terms of limiting and horizon subgradients.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is locally lsc at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar\partial f(\bar x)\text{ and }\bar\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\text{ have the stated closed-convex, polar, recession, support, and pointed-cone representations}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(x\in U\), and let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz near \(x\) with constant \(L\). For every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), each sufficiently small \(t>0\) satisfies \(|(f(x+td)-f(x))/t|\le L\|d\|\). Thus any existing ordinary directional derivative is finite, but local Lipschitz continuity alone does not ensure that the limit exists. Directional differentiability supplies existence; a local Lipschitz bound supplies finiteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitz continuity bounds directional quotients and guarantees finiteness only when their limit exists; directional differentiability is a separate requirement.

knowledge_statements.title: Direction Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional directional derivatives; instability is discontinuity in the direction argument at a fixed base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Direction instability occurs at \((x,d)\) when \(f'(x;d)\) exists and there is a sequence \(d_k\to d\) such that every \(f'(x;d_k)\) exists but \(f'(x;d_k)\not\to f'(x;d)\). Equivalently, the mapping \(v\mapsto f'(x;v)\), restricted to the directions where the derivative exists and is finite, is not continuous at \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direction instability means that directional derivatives along directions converging to a fixed direction fail to converge to the derivative in that limiting direction.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space, \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and the finite one-sided directional derivative \(f'(x;d)\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of directional derivatives does not by itself imply continuity with respect to the direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexification is information-losing whenever \(D\ne\overline{\operatorname{co}}D\): points of \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}D\setminus D\) become indistinguishable from genuine directions after replacement. For example, if \(D=\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\), then \((1/2,1/2)\in\operatorname{co}D\) although \((1/2,1/2)\notin D\). Nevertheless, every linear probe is preserved in the sense that \(\sigma_D(z)=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}D}(z)\) for all \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). Hence support-function or polar data cannot reconstruct the original nonconvex directional set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexification adds averaged directions and preserves all linear support values, so support or polar data cannot recover the original nonconvex directional structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential characterizations of contingent and Clarke tangent cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts existential approximation at a fixed base point with uniform approximation from arbitrary nearby feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x\in S\subset\mathbf E. A vector h belongs to K_S(x) if and only if there exist sequences t_r\downarrow0 and h^r\to h such that x+t_rh^r\in S for every r. A vector h belongs to T_S(x) if and only if, for every pair of sequences t_r\downarrow0 and x^r\to x with x^r\in S, there exists a sequence h^r\to h such that x^r+t_rh^r\in S for every r.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is contingent when it can be approximated along some vanishing step sequence from x. It is Clarke tangent when such approximating directions exist for every vanishing step sequence and every feasible sequence approaching x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\in K_S(x)\iff\exists(t_r\downarrow0)\,\exists(h^r\to h)\,\forall r:\ x+t_rh^r\in S;\quad h\in T_S(x)\iff\forall(t_r\downarrow0)\,\forall(x^r\in S,\ x^r\to x)\,\exists(h^r\to h)\,\forall r:\ x^r+t_rh^r\in S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limit Relations Between Tangent Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relations at a locally closed set in a Banach space, with additional reflexivity and norm-regularity conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be a Banach space and let \Omega\subset X be locally closed around \bar x. Then \operatorname*{Liminf}_{x\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x}T(x;\Omega)\subset T_C(\bar x;\Omega). If X is reflexive, then also T_C(\bar x;\Omega)\subset\operatorname*{Liminf}_{x\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x}T_W(x;\Omega). If, moreover, the norm of X is Kadec and Fréchet differentiable away from the origin, then T_C(\bar x;\Omega)=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{x\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x}T_W(x;\Omega).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a set locally closed near x-bar in a Banach space, the lower set limit of nearby contingent cones is contained in the Clarke tangent cone. In a reflexive space, the Clarke tangent cone is contained in the lower limit of nearby weak contingent cones. If the norm is also Kadec and Fréchet differentiable away from zero, the latter inclusion is equality.
assumptions_latex: \Omega\subset X\text{ is locally closed around }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{Liminf}_{x\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x}T(x;\Omega)\subset T_C(\bar x;\Omega),\quad X\text{ reflexive}\Rightarrow T_C(\bar x;\Omega)\subset\operatorname*{Liminf}_{x\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x}T_W(x;\Omega),\quad \bigl(\|\cdot\|\text{ Kadec and Fréchet differentiable on }X\setminus\{0\}\bigr)\Rightarrow T_C(\bar x;\Omega)=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{x\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x}T_W(x;\Omega).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the contingent cone through the lower Dini derivative and records the convex-set representation and Clarke comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For x\in S\subset\mathbf E, K_S(x)=\{h\in\mathbf E:d_S^{-}(x;h)=0\}. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contingent, Weak Contingent, and Clarke Tangent Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a set in a Banach space at one of its points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Omega\subset X and \bar x\in\Omega. The contingent cone is T(\bar x;\Omega):=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{t\downarrow0}(\Omega-\bar x)/t, with the outer limit taken in the norm topology. The weak contingent cone T_W(\bar x;\Omega) is defined by the same formula with the outer limit taken in the weak topology. The Clarke tangent cone is T_C(\bar x;\Omega):=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{x\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x,\,t\downarrow0}(\Omega-x)/t, with the inner limit taken in the norm topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a subset Ω of a Banach space and a point x-bar in Ω, the contingent cone is the norm-topology outer limit of (Ω−x-bar)/t as t decreases to zero. Replacing norm convergence by weak convergence gives the weak contingent cone. The Clarke tangent cone is the norm-topology inner limit of (Ω−x)/t as x approaches x-bar within Ω and t decreases to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(\bar x;\Omega)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\Omega-\bar x}{t},\quad T_W(\bar x;\Omega)=\operatorname*{w-Limsup}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\Omega-\bar x}{t},\quad T_C(\bar x;\Omega)=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{x\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x,\,t\downarrow0}\frac{\Omega-x}{t}.

Consequently \(T_C^{\mathrm a}(x)\subset T_C(x)\).

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a subset of a finite-dimensional normed space \(X\), and \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inner tangent cone records directions whose nearby rays remain inside the set for all sufficiently small steps.

notation.meaning: radial inner tangent cone to C at x under the stated convention

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the radial eventual-feasibility convention; literature uses “inner tangent” for several inequivalent cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the radial eventual-feasibility convention, the inner tangent cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is \[T_C^{\mathrm i}(x):=\left\{v\in X:\exists\,\varepsilon>0\ \text{such that}\ x+t v\in C\ \text{for every}\ t\in[0,\varepsilon]\right\}.\] It is positively homogeneous and satisfies \(T_C^{\mathrm i}(x)\subset T_C^{\mathrm a}(x)\subset T_C(x)\). The first inclusion can be strict because adjacent tangency permits scale-dependent corrections to the direction, whereas radial inner tangency requires the unperturbed ray itself to remain feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the radial convention, an inner tangent direction keeps the exact short ray from the base point feasible, a stronger requirement than adjacent tangency.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner and Outer Second-Order Tangent Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a subset of a normed space, at a base point and along a prescribed direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S\subset X\), \(x\in S\), and \(h\in X\), define
\[
T_S^{i,2}(x,h):=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{S-x-th}{\tfrac12t^2},\qquad T_S^2(x,h):=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{S-x-th}{\tfrac12t^2}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
T_S^{i,2}(x,h)=\{w:\operatorname{dist}(x+th+\tfrac12t^2w,S)=o(t^2)\text{ as }t\downarrow0\},
\]
while \(w\in T_S^2(x,h)\) iff this distance condition holds along some sequence \(t_n\downarrow0\). These sets are closed and \(T_S^{i,2}(x,h)\subseteq T_S^2(x,h)\). Nonemptiness of the inner set implies \(h\in T_S^i(x)\), and nonemptiness of the outer set implies \(h\in T_S(x)\). If \(S\) is convex, then \(T_S^{i,2}(x,h)\) is convex, whereas \(T_S^2(x,h)\) need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner and outer second-order tangent sets are the lower and upper set limits of the quadratically rescaled residual sets. They admit equivalent distance characterizations, are closed, and the inner set is contained in the outer set. Their nonemptiness requires the direction to lie in the corresponding first-order tangent set. For convex S the inner second-order tangent set is convex, but the outer one can be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_S^{i,2}(x,h)\subseteq T_S^2(x,h),\quad T_S^{i,2}(x,h)\text{ and }T_S^2(x,h)\text{ are closed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{epi}g\subset\mathbb R^2\), where \(g(s)=s^2\), and let \(x=(0,0)\). For \(v=(1,0)\) and every \(t>0\), the point \((t,t^2)\in C\) satisfies \((t,t^2)/t=(1,t)\to(1,0)\); hence \(v\in T_C^{\mathrm a}(x)\). But \(x+t v=(t,0)\notin C\) for every \(t>0\), so \(v\notin T_C^{\mathrm i}(x)\). Therefore \(T_C^{\mathrm i}(x)\subsetneq T_C^{\mathrm a}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the parabola epigraph at its vertex, the horizontal direction is adjacent tangent but its exact ray is never feasible, creating a strict gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Clarke tangent cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is the set of all \(v\in X\) such that, whenever \(x_k\in C\), \(x_k\to x\), and \(t_k\downarrow0\), there exist \(v_k\to v\) with \(x_k+t_kv_k\in C\) for every \(k\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke tangent cone and its necessary optimality condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the cone through the Clarke derivative of the distance function, records its geometry, and conditionally states the associated first-order necessary condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For x\in S\subset\mathbf E, define T_S(x)=\{h\in\mathbf E:d_S^{\circ}(x;h)=0\}. Because d_S^{\circ}(x;\cdot) is finite, nonnegative, and sublinear, T_S(x) is a closed convex cone. If, additionally, f is locally Lipschitz near x and x is a local minimizer of f on S, then for every sufficiently large L\ge0 and every h\in\mathbf E, 0\le (f+Ld_S)^{\circ}(x;h)\le f^{\circ}(x;h)+L d_S^{\circ}(x;h); consequently, h\in T_S(x) implies f^{\circ}(x;h)\ge0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke tangent cone is the set of directions where the Clarke derivative of the distance function vanishes, and it is a closed convex cone. For a locally Lipschitz objective at a constrained local minimum, its Clarke directional derivative is nonnegative in every Clarke tangent direction.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the optimality conclusion, }f:\mathbf E\to\mathbf R\text{ is locally Lipschitz near }x
\text{For the optimality conclusion, }x\text{ is a local minimizer of }f\text{ on }S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_S(x)=\{h:d_S^{\circ}(x;h)=0\}\text{ is a closed convex cone};\qquad h\in T_S(x)\Rightarrow f^{\circ}(x;h)\ge0\text{ under the stated optimality assumptions}.

knowledge_statements.title: Linearization Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abadie-type exactness for smooth finite-dimensional equality-and-inequality constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Linearization is exact at \(\bar x\) when \[T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x).\] For a differentiable equality-and-inequality constraint system, one always has \(T_C(\bar x)\subset L_C(\bar x)\). Consequently, exactness is equivalent to the reverse inclusion \(L_C(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\); this equality is Abadie’s constraint qualification at \(\bar x\). Any stronger constraint qualification known to imply Abadie’s condition therefore guarantees linearization exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearization is exact when every direction satisfying the first-order constraint system is a contingent tangent direction, so the tangent and linearized cones coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ h_j(x)=0,\ j=1,\ldots,p\}\), the constraint functions are differentiable at \(\bar x\in C\), and \(L_C(\bar x)\) is the corresponding linearized cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Linearization is exact at \(\bar x\) if and only if \(T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bouligand Tangent, Regular Normal, and Limiting Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional tangent and normal-cone definitions, with the convex-set specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and \(\bar z\in\Omega\), \(T_\Omega(\bar z)=\{u\in\mathbb R^d\mid \exists t_k\downarrow0,\ u_k\to u,\ \bar z+t_ku_k\in\Omega\ \forall k\}\). The regular normal cone is \(\widehat N_\Omega(\bar z)=T_\Omega(\bar z)^\circ\), and \(N_\Omega(\bar z)=\{z^*\mid \exists z_k\in\Omega,\ z_k\to\bar z,\ z_k^*\to z^*,\ z_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(z_k)\ \forall k\}\). If \(\Omega\) is convex, then \(\widehat N_\Omega(\bar z)=N_\Omega(\bar z)=\{z^*\mid \langle z^*,z-\bar z\rangle\leq0\ \forall z\in\Omega\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bouligand tangent cone consists of sequential limits of feasible infinitesimal directions. Its polar is the regular normal cone, while limiting normals are limits of regular normals at nearby feasible points. For a convex set, both normal cones equal the classical convex normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat N_\Omega(\bar z)=T_\Omega(\bar z)^\circ,\qquad N_\Omega(\bar z)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{z\to_\Omega\bar z}\widehat N_\Omega(z),\qquad \Omega\text{ convex}\Rightarrow \widehat N_\Omega(\bar z)=N_\Omega(\bar z)=\{z^*:\langle z^*,z-\bar z\rangle\leq0\ \forall z\in\Omega\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-analytic normal cone for closed convex sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex normal cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is \[N_C(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\ \text{for every}\ y\in C\right\}.\] If \(x\notin C\), set \(N_C(x):=\varnothing\). For \(x\in C\), the set \(N_C(x)\) is a closed convex cone and satisfies \(N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\). Every nonzero \(v\in N_C(x)\) is the normal of a supporting hyperplane to \(C\) through \(x\); the zero vector also belongs to \(N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex normal has nonpositive inner product with every feasible displacement from the base point; each nonzero convex normal defines a supporting hyperplane there.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of \(\mathbb R^n\), and \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convex normal cone consists of the zero vector together with all nonzero vectors defining supporting hyperplanes to \(C\) at \(x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Normal Cone and Tangent-Cone Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the extract's nonnegative polar convention and includes the empty-value extension outside the closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be convex and x\in\operatorname{cl}\Omega. Define N_\Omega(x):=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle\xi,y-x\rangle\le0\ \text{for all }y\in\Omega\}. For K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, let K^*:=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle\xi,k\rangle\ge0\ \text{for all }k\in K\}. Then N_\Omega(x)=-(T_\Omega(x))^*. Extend the normal-cone multifunction by N_\Omega(y):=\varnothing whenever y\notin\operatorname{cl}\Omega.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Normal Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the support-based normal cone at a point of a closed convex set, including its positive-scaling property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex, and let \(x\in\Omega\). The normal cone to \(\Omega\) at \(x\) is
\[
N_\Omega(x)=\left\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:d^T(y-x)\leq 0\text{ for all }y\in\Omega\right\}.
\]
If \(d\in N_\Omega(x)\) and \(t>0\), then \(td\in N_\Omega(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set Omega and a point x in Omega, the normal cone contains exactly the vectors whose inner product with every feasible displacement from x is nonpositive. It is closed under positive scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_\Omega(x)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:d^T(y-x)\leq0\ \forall y\in\Omega\},\qquad d\in N_\Omega(x),\ t>0\Rightarrow td\in N_\Omega(x).

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean proximal normals defined through metric projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(x\in C\). The proximal normal cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is
\[
N_C^P(x):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\ x\in P_C(x+r v)\text{ for some }r>0\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in N_C^P(x)\) precisely when some \(r>0\) satisfies
\[
\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq \frac{1}{2r}\|y-x\|^2\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
In particular, \(N_C^P(x)\) is a cone containing the zero vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is proximal normal when moving from the point in that direction leaves the point as a nearest point of the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^P(x)=\{v:x\in P_C(x+r v)\text{ for some }r>0\}\).

notation.meaning: set of Euclidean nearest points in C to z

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fréchet normals for locally closed subsets of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(x\in C\). The regular, or Fréchet, normal cone is
\[
\widehat N_C(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\limsup_{\substack{y\to x,\ y\in C\\y\neq x}}\frac{\langle v,y-x\rangle}{\|y-x\|}\leq0\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in\widehat N_C(x)\) when
\[
\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq o(\|y-x\|)\quad\text{as }y\to x\text{ within }C.
\]
Thus regular normals are first-order supporting vectors at the specified point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular normal makes a nonpositive first-order angle with every feasible displacement approaching the base point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(x)=\{v:\limsup_{y\to x,\,y\in C\setminus\{x\}}\langle v,y-x\rangle/\|y-x\|\leq0\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mordukhovich normals obtained as outer limits of regular normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(x\in C\). The limiting, or Mordukhovich, normal cone is
\[
N_C(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exist }x_k\to x\text{ with }x_k\in C,\\ v_k\to v\text{ with }v_k\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\end{array}\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(N_C(x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{y\to x,\,y\in C}\widehat N_C(y)\). The cone \(N_C(x)\) is closed but need not be convex, and it always contains \(\widehat N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limiting normals are limits of regular normals taken at nearby feasible points; the resulting cone can be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{y\to x,\,y\in C}\widehat N_C(y)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convexification of the limiting normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(x\in C\). The Clarke normal cone is the closed convex hull of the limiting normal cone:
\[
N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}N_C(x).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\widehat N_C(x)\subset N_C(x)\subset N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x),
\]
and \(N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)\) is always a closed convex cone. Convexification may discard the branch-sensitive, nonconvex structure retained by limiting normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke normal cone is the closed convex hull of all limiting normals and is therefore closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}N_C(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of Local Epigraph Recession Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equates local epigraph recession membership with uniform local bounds expressed through subderivatives, subgradients, and finite increments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be finite and locally lower semicontinuous at \(\bar x\), and let \((w,\beta)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\). The following are equivalent:
\[
(w,\beta)\in R_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x));
\]
there exist a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\delta>0\) such that, for every \(x\in V\) with \(f(x)\leq f(\bar x)+\delta\), respectively,
\[
df(x)(w)\leq\beta,\qquad \widehat d f(x)(w)\leq\beta,
\]
\[
\langle v,w\rangle\leq\beta\quad\forall v\in\partial f(x),\qquad
\langle v,w\rangle\leq\beta\quad\forall v\in\widehat\partial f(x);
\]
and there exist a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\delta,\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[
\frac{f(x+\tau w)-f(x)}{\tau}\leq\beta
\]
for every \(x\in V\) satisfying \(f(x)\leq f(\bar x)+\delta\) and every \(\tau\in(0,\varepsilon]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pair (w,β) is a local recession direction of the epigraph at (x̄,f(x̄)) exactly when, uniformly near x̄ and on a sufficiently small upper level set, β bounds either subderivative in direction w, bounds the pairing of w with every limiting or regular subgradient, or bounds all sufficiently short forward difference quotients along w.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is finite and locally lsc at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (a)--(f), comprising local epigraph recession membership and the stated uniform derivative, subgradient, and increment bounds, are equivalent}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Subgradient and Clarke Horizon Subgradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the two Clarke subdifferential objects through the Clarke normal cone to the epigraph at a finite point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an extended-real-valued function \(f\) finite at \(\bar x\), let \(\bar N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{con}N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\). The Clarke subdifferential and Clarke horizon subdifferential are
\[
\bar\partial f(\bar x):=\{v\mid (v,-1)\in\bar N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\},\qquad

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Tangent–Normal Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact polar duality for a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(x\in C\). Define
\[
T_C(x):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-x),\qquad K^\circ:=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,d\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }d\in K\}.
\]
Then the convex normal and tangent cones are exact polar duals:
\[
N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(x)=T_C(x)^\circ,
\qquad
T_C(x)=N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(x)^\circ.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a closed convex set, the tangent and normal cones are mutual negative polars.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\) and \(T_C(x)=N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(x)^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polarity between Bouligand tangents and regular normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(x\in C\), and define the Bouligand tangent cone by
\[
T_C(x):=\{d:\exists\,t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d\text{ with }x+t_kd_k\in C\}.
\]
With the negative-polar convention \(K^\circ:=\{v:\langle v,d\rangle\leq0\ \forall d\in K\}\), the regular normal cone satisfies the exact identity
\[
\widehat N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ.
\]
The reverse polar gives \(\widehat N_C(x)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}T_C(x)\), which need not equal the generally nonconvex cone \(T_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular normals are exactly the negative polar of the Bouligand tangent cone; reversing polarity convexifies the tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact polarity between Clarke tangent and normal cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(x\in C\). Its Clarke tangent cone consists of vectors \(d\) such that, for every \(x_k\to x\) in \(C\) and every \(t_k\downarrow0\), there exist \(d_k\to d\) with \(x_k+t_kd_k\in C\). Then
\[
N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\bigl(T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)\bigr)^\circ,
\qquad
T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\bigl(N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)\bigr)^\circ,
\]
where \(K^\circ:=\{v:\langle v,d\rangle\leq0\text{ for all }d\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke tangent and Clarke normal cones are closed convex cones that are exact negative polars of one another.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=(T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x))^\circ\) and \(T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=(N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x))^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.title: Regular–Clarke Polarity Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A crossing set exhibits strict regular-to-Clarke enlargement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C:=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R)\subset\mathbb R^2,
\qquad x=(0,0).
\]
Its Bouligand tangent cone is \(T_C(x)=C\), hence regular polarity gives
\[
\widehat N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ=\{0\}.
\]
Normals obtained along either branch yield
\[
N_C(x)=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R),
\qquad N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\mathbb R^2.
\]
Thus \(\widehat N_C(x)\subsetneq N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)\), while the Clarke tangent cone is \(T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the crossing of two coordinate axes, the regular normal is zero but the Clarke normal fills the plane.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the union of the two coordinate axes in \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(x)=\{0\}\subsetneq N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\mathbb R^2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Normals beyond Exact Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex limiting normals cannot generally be recovered by one polar operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every set \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\), its negative polar \(K^\circ\) is a closed convex cone. A limiting normal cone need not be convex and therefore need not equal the polar of any tangent-like set. For example, for
\[
C:=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R),\qquad x=(0,0),
\]
one has
\[
N_C(x)=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R),
\]
which is nonconvex. Hence no set \(K\) satisfies \(N_C(x)=K^\circ\); polarity instead describes regular or Clarke normals after the appropriate convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because every polar cone is convex, a nonconvex limiting normal cone cannot be represented as one polar cone.
assumptions_latex: Negative polarity is defined by \(K^\circ=\{v:\langle v,d\rangle\leq0\ \forall d\in K\}\).
The ambient space is finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(x)\) need not equal \(K^\circ\) for any set \(K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke-Regular Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone definition of Clarke regularity at a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\). The set \(C\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar x\) when its regular and limiting normal cones agree:
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x).
\]
Equivalently, every limiting normal generated by nearby points already satisfies the first-order regular-normal inequality at \(\bar x\). Under this equality the common cone is convex and also equals the Clarke normal cone:
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)=N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is Clarke regular at a point when every limiting normal there is already a regular normal.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is Clarke regular at }\bar x\iff\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local convexity implies normal regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion and normal-cone representation are local to the specified neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space, let \(\bar x\in\Omega\subset X\), and let \(U\) be a neighborhood of \(\bar x\) such that \(\Omega\cap U\) is convex. Then \(\Omega\) is normally regular at \(\bar x\), and
\[
N(\bar x;\Omega)=\left\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,x-\bar x\rangle\le 0\ \text{for every }x\in\Omega\cap U\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a set is convex in a neighborhood of the reference point, it is normally regular there, and its normal cone is characterized by the supporting inequality on that local convex portion.
assumptions_latex: U\text{ is a neighborhood of }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N(\bar x;\Omega)=\widehat N(\bar x;\Omega)=\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,x-\bar x\rangle\le 0\ \forall x\in\Omega\cap U\}

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform local quadratic support formulation of prox-regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\). The set \(C\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(r>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, whenever \(x,y\in C\cap B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) and \(v\in N_C(x)\) with \(\|v\|=1\),
\[
\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2r}\|y-x\|^2.
\]
Thus every nearby unit limiting normal supports \(C\) with one uniform quadratic curvature bound. If the condition holds at every point of \(C\), then \(C\) is called a prox-regular set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is prox-regular when all nearby unit limiting normals obey a uniform local quadratic support inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists r,\varepsilon>0\ \forall x,y,v:\ \langle v,y-x\rangle\leq\|y-x\|^2/(2r)\) under the stated local conditions.

notation.meaning: open Euclidean ball of radius epsilon

knowledge_statements.title: Subsmooth Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definition using the limiting normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is subsmooth at \(\bar x\in C\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge -\varepsilon\|x_1-x_2\|
\]
whenever \(x_1,x_2\in C\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\) and \(v_i\in N_C(x_i)\cap\mathbb B\) for \(i=1,2\). It is locally subsmooth on \(C\) if it is subsmooth at every point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed set is subsmooth when its unit limiting normals satisfy a local approximate monotonicity inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge-\varepsilon\|x_1-x_2\|\) locally for unit limiting normals.

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to C at x
open ball of radius delta about bar x

review_flags: Exact source for the limiting-normal formulation of subsmoothness is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Subsmooth Sets container and is internally well formed, but no citation is supplied. A direct source is required because subsmoothness conventions vary with the chosen normal cone and ambient setting.

children.title: Superregular Sets

knowledge_statements.title: Superregular Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise finite-dimensional superregularity in normal-cone form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is superregular at \(\bar x\in C\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\langle v,z-x\rangle\le \varepsilon\|v\|\,\|z-x\|
\]
for all \(x,z\in C\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\) and every \(v\in N_C(x)\). Thus nearby normal vectors make, up to an arbitrarily small relative error, nonacute angles with displacements directed from their base points into the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Superregularity bounds every nearby normal’s outward component along chords joining nearby points of the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle v,z-x\rangle\le\varepsilon\|v\|\|z-x\|\) for all sufficiently nearby admissible \(x,z,v\).

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to C at x
open ball of radius delta about bar x

review_flags: Exact source fixing the normal-cone convention for superregularity is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normal-cone inequality is a plausible finite-dimensional definition of superregularity, but the convention needs a direct source. In addition, the final sentence's description as a nonacute-angle condition is inconsistent with the displayed upper bound, which expresses an approximately nonpositive inner product.

children.title: Subsmooth–Superregular Comparison
children.top_down_role: Inclusion and separation regimes between the two regularity classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Subsmooth–Superregular Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence under the shared finite-dimensional limiting-normal convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be closed and let \(\bar x\in C\). Under the displayed limiting-normal definitions, \(C\) is subsmooth at \(\bar x\) if and only if it is superregular at \(\bar x\). Indeed, the subsmooth inequality with one normal set to zero yields the superregular inequality after scaling; conversely, applying superregularity to each of two unit normals and adding the resulting inequalities gives
\[
\langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge-2\eta\|x_1-x_2\|,
\]
where \(\eta\) may be chosen as \(\varepsilon/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With limiting normals in finite dimensions, subsmoothness and superregularity are equivalent local regularity properties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is subsmooth at }\bar x\iff C\text{ is superregular at }\bar x\).

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone used in both definitions

review_flags: A source explicitly establishing equivalence under identical normal-cone conventions is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison belongs in this property container, but the equivalence depends on using exactly compatible normal-cone definitions and is unsupported by a citation. The sentences beginning with "Indeed" also constitute proof text and must be removed from any sourced replacement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local smooth inverse-image definition with convex target and basic constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is amenable at \(\bar x\in C\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), a continuously differentiable mapping \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\), and a closed convex set \(D\subset\mathbb R^m\) such that
\[
C\cap U=\{x\in U:F(x)\in D\},
\]
and the basic constraint qualification
\[
N_D(F(\bar x))\cap\ker \nabla F(\bar x)^*=\{0\}
\]
holds. The set is amenable if it is amenable at each of its points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An amenable set is locally a smooth inverse image of a closed convex set satisfying a normal-cone constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap U=F^{-1}(D)\cap U\) and \(N_D(F(\bar x))\cap\ker\nabla F(\bar x)^*=\{0\}\).

adjoint of the derivative of F at bar x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Amenable and fully amenable sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local smooth inverse-image representation with a normal-cone transversality qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(Q\subset\mathbf E\) is amenable at \(\bar{x}\in Q\) if there exist an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar{x}\), a Euclidean space \(\mathbf Y\), a closed convex set \(R\subset\mathbf Y\), and a continuously differentiable map \(h:U\to\mathbf Y\) such that \[Q\cap U=h^{-1}(R)\] and \[N_R(h(\bar{x}))\cap\ker((\nabla h(\bar{x}))^*)=\{0\}.\] It is fully amenable at \(\bar{x}\) if \(h\) can be chosen twice continuously differentiable at \(\bar{x}\). The transversality condition also holds after replacing \(\bar{x}\) by any sufficiently nearby point of \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is amenable at a point if it is locally the inverse image of a closed convex set under a continuously differentiable map satisfying a normal-cone transversality condition. It is fully amenable if the map can be chosen twice continuously differentiable. The qualification persists at nearby points of the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\cap U=h^{-1}(R),\quad R\text{ is closed and convex},\quad N_R(h(\bar{x}))\cap\ker((\nabla h(\bar{x}))^*)=\{0\};\quad h\text{ twice continuously differentiable at }\bar{x}\text{ yields full amenability, and the qualification persists locally on }Q.

knowledge_statements.title: Subamenable Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local smooth inverse-image definition using metric subregularity instead of the basic qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is subamenable at \(\bar x\in C\) if, on some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), there exist a continuously differentiable mapping \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) and a closed convex set \(D\subset\mathbb R^m\) such that \(C\cap U=\{x\in U:F(x)\in D\}\), and constants \(\kappa,r>0\) satisfy
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D)
\quad\text{for all }x\in B_r(\bar x).
\]
This inequality is metric subregularity of the associated constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subamenable set has a smooth convex constraint representation whose residual locally bounds distance to feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D)\) locally around \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Amenability Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local implication between amenability and subamenability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\). If \(C\) is amenable at \(\bar x\), then \(C\) is subamenable at \(\bar x\). In particular, for a local representation \(C=F^{-1}(D)\) with \(D\) closed and convex, the qualification
\[
N_D(F(\bar x))\cap\ker\nabla F(\bar x)^*=\{0\}
\]
implies a local error bound
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D).
\]
The reverse implication need not hold because metric subregularity is weaker than the displayed qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Amenability implies subamenability; the converse can fail because a local error bound need not imply the basic constraint qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is amenable at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ amenable at }\bar x\Longrightarrow C\text{ subamenable at }\bar x\), while the converse is not automatic.
review_flags: Direct support is needed for the implication and strictness of the hierarchy.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-normal polarity for a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(x\in C\). Its tangent and normal cones satisfy
\[
T_C(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-x),
\qquad
N_C(x)=\{v:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\ \text{for all }y\in C\},
\]
and are polar to one another:
\[
N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ,
\qquad
T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ.
\]
Consequently, the regular, limiting, and convex-analytic normal cones coincide at every point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set, tangent and normal cones are mutual polars, and the standard normal-cone constructions coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\) and \(T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Theorem for Nonempty Closed Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, and variational characterization of Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(y\notin S\). There exists a unique \(\bar x\in S\) such that \[\|y-\bar x\|=\inf_{x\in S}\|y-x\|.\] Moreover, for \(\bar x\in S\), \[\bar x=P_S(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle y-\bar x,x-\bar x\rangle\le 0\quad\text{for every }x\in S.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point outside a nonempty closed convex subset of Euclidean space has a unique nearest point in the set. A point in the set is this projection exactly when the displacement from it to the external point has nonpositive inner product with every displacement toward another point of the set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separating, properly separating, strictly separating, and strongly separating hyperplanes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four separation notions for two nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_1,S_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty convex sets, let \(p\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(H=\{x:p^Tx=\alpha\}\). The hyperplane \(H\) separates \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) if \(p^Tx\ge\alpha\) for all \(x\in S_1\) and \(p^Tx\le\alpha\) for all \(x\in S_2\). It properly separates them if it separates them and \(S_1\cup S_2\not\subseteq H\). It strictly separates them if \(p^Tx>\alpha\) for all \(x\in S_1\) and \(p^Tx<\alpha\) for all \(x\in S_2\). It strongly separates them if there exists \(\epsilon>0\) such that \(p^Tx\ge\alpha+\epsilon\) for all \(x\in S_1\) and \(p^Tx\le\alpha\) for all \(x\in S_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperplane separates two nonempty convex sets when the sets lie in its opposite closed halfspaces; separation is proper when their union is not contained in the hyperplane, strict when both inequalities are strict, and strong when a positive uniform margin separates the first set from the hyperplane while the second remains in the opposite closed halfspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}H\text{ separates }S_1,S_2&\iff (\forall x\in S_1\;p^Tx\ge\alpha)\land(\forall x\in S_2\;p^Tx\le\alpha),\\H\text{ properly separates }S_1,S_2&\iff H\text{ separates }S_1,S_2\land S_1\cup S_2\not\subseteq H,\\H\text{ strictly separates }S_1,S_2&\iff (\forall x\in S_1\;p^Tx>\alpha)\land(\forall x\in S_2\;p^Tx<\alpha),\\H\text{ strongly separates }S_1,S_2&\iff \exists\epsilon>0:\;(\forall x\in S_1\;p^Tx\ge\alpha+\epsilon)\land(\forall x\in S_2\;p^Tx\le\alpha).\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hulls, Cones, and Convex Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary characterizations of convex hulls and convex cones under the source's convention that cone scaling uses \lambda>0.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, \operatorname{conv}(S)=\bigcap\{D:S\subseteq D,\ D\text{ is convex}\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i:m\geq1,\ x_i\in S,\ \alpha_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1\right\}, and this is the smallest convex set containing S. A nonempty C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n is a cone if x\in C implies \lambda x\in C for every \lambda>0; it is a convex cone if it is also convex. Under this convention, C is a convex cone if and only if it is closed under addition and positive scalar multiplication. If S is nonempty and convex, then \{\lambda x:\lambda>0,\ x\in S\} is the smallest convex cone containing S.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull is the intersection of all convex supersets and equivalently the set of finite convex combinations. A cone is closed under positive scaling, and a convex cone is equivalently closed under addition and positive scaling. For a nonempty convex set, its positive-scaling hull is the smallest convex cone containing it under the source's convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(S)=\bigcap\{D:S\subseteq D,\ D\text{ convex}\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i:x_i\in S,\ \alpha_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\alpha_i=1\right\};\quad C\text{ is a convex cone}\iff C+C\subseteq C\text{ and }\lambda C\subseteq C\ (\lambda>0);\quad S\text{ convex}\Rightarrow \{\lambda x:\lambda>0,\ x\in S\}\text{ is the smallest convex cone containing }S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicator Function of a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the extended-real indicator and records its basic convex-analytic properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite inequality-equality representation and active-set cone formulas.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Convex Polyhedra p. 95

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^p\), \(E\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), and \(f\in\mathbb R^q\), and let
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Ex=f\}
\]
be a nonempty convex polyhedron. For \(x\in P\), write \(a_i^T\) for the \(i\)-th row of \(A\) and define \(I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:a_i^Tx=b_i\}\). Then
\[
T_P(x)=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:a_i^Td\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x),\ Ed=0\},
\]
and
\[
N_P(x)=\{A_{I(x)}^T\lambda+E^T\mu:\lambda\in\mathbb R^{|I(x)|}_+,\ \mu\in\mathbb R^q\}.
\]
Thus both cones are polyhedral and are determined by the constraints active at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedron defined by finitely many inequalities and equalities, the tangent and normal cones have explicit representations determined by the active inequalities and the equality constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact local first-order geometry of convex polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty convex polyhedron \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in P\), there exists \(r>0\) such that
\[
(P-x)\cap B_r(0)=T_P(x)\cap B_r(0).
\]
Hence the local feasible geometry is exactly conical, the tangent cone is closed and polyhedral, and
\[
\widehat N_P(x)=N_P(x)=T_P(x)^\circ.
\]
Moreover, the normal-cone mapping is constant on the relative interior of each face and is determined by the inequalities active on that face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near each point, a convex polyhedron agrees with its tangent cone; its regular and limiting normals coincide and are facewise constant.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((P-x)\cap B_r(0)=T_P(x)\cap B_r(0)\) for some \(r>0\), and \(\widehat N_P(x)=N_P(x)\).

notation.meaning: regular normal cone to P at x
limiting normal cone to P at x
tangent cone to P at x

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Manifold Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical tangent and normal spaces for an embedded smooth manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a continuously differentiable embedded manifold near \(\bar x\in M\). If locally
\[
M=\{x:F(x)=0\},
\]
where \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable and \(\nabla F(\bar x)\) has full row rank, then
\[
T_M(\bar x)=\ker\nabla F(\bar x),
\qquad
N_M(\bar x)=T_M(\bar x)^\perp=\operatorname{range}\nabla F(\bar x)^*.
\]
The regular and limiting normal cones both equal this classical normal space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth embedded manifold, the tangent space is the constraint Jacobian’s kernel and the normal space is its adjoint range.
assumptions_latex: \(M\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a continuously differentiable embedded manifold near \(\bar x\).
\(M\) is locally the zero set of a full-row-rank mapping \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_M(\bar x)=\ker\nabla F(\bar x)\) and \(N_M(\bar x)=\operatorname{range}\nabla F(\bar x)^*\).

notation.meaning: classical tangent space to M at bar x
classical and generalized normal space at bar x
adjoint of a linear mapping L

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local and Global Smooth Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an embedded manifold locally as a regular level set of a twice continuously differentiable map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(M\subset\mathbf E\) is a manifold of codimension \(m\) around \(\bar x\in M\) if there exist a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\) and a \(C^2\) map \(F:V\to\mathbb R^m\) such that \(\nabla F(\bar x)\) is surjective and, for every \(z\in V\), \(z\in M\iff F(z)=0\). The set \(M\) is a manifold of codimension \(m\) if this condition holds around every \(\bar x\in M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is a codimension-m manifold near a point if it is locally the zero set of a twice continuously differentiable map whose derivative at that point is surjective. It is a manifold if this holds at every point of the set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-independence criterion for rank-stratum transversality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a coordinate criterion for transversality of a differentiable symmetric-matrix-valued map to \(\mathcal W_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(G(x)\in\mathcal W_r\), so \(\operatorname{rank}G(x)=r\), and let \(e_1,\ldots,e_{p-r}\) be a basis of \(\ker G(x)\). knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Union Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent and limiting-normal calculus for a finite union of closed sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\bigcup_{i=1}^p C_i\), where every \(C_i\subset\mathbb R^n\) is closed, and let \(I(x)=\{i:x\in C_i\}\). Then
\[
T_C(x)=\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}T_{C_i}(x)
\]
and
\[
N_C(x)\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}N_{C_i}(x).
\]
The normal inclusion may be strict because regular normals to the union must respect all locally active pieces before passage to limiting normals. Thus tangent directions select an active piece, whereas normal behavior records interactions among active pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite union’s tangent cone is the union of active-piece tangents, while its limiting normals lie among active-piece limiting normals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C(x)=\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}T_{C_i}(x)\) and \(N_C(x)\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}N_{C_i}(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional disjunctive feasible sets with polyhedral alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) has disjunctive geometry near \(\bar x\in C\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\), a continuously differentiable mapping \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\), and a finite union of convex polyhedra
\[
D=\bigcup_{j=1}^q D_j
\]
such that
\[
C\cap U=\{x\in U:F(x)\in D\}.
\]
The active disjuncts at \(\bar x\) are indexed by \(J(\bar x)=\{j:F(\bar x)\in D_j\}\); local tangent and normal formulas depend on these pieces and on a suitable qualification for the inverse-image system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjunctive geometry represents a feasible set locally as the smooth inverse image of a finite union of convex polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap U=\{x\in U:F(x)\in\bigcup_{j=1}^qD_j\}\) with each \(D_j\) convex polyhedral.

notation.meaning: indices of disjuncts active at bar x

Then the Bouligand tangent cone satisfies \[T_C(\bar x)=\bigcup_{i\in I(\bar x)}T_{C_i}(\bar x).\] Consequently, by polarity of the regular normal and tangent cones, \[\widehat N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^\circ=\bigcap_{i\in I(\bar x)}\widehat N_{C_i}(\bar x).\] Thus primal feasible directions combine by union, whereas regular dual constraints combine by intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a finite union, tangent directions come from active pieces, while regular normals must be normal to every active piece.

children.title: Spectral Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometry induced by eigenvalue and singular-value structure.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{S}^n\) carries the Frobenius inner product, and \(\lambda(X)\) lists the eigenvalues of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The spectral lift is \(\Lambda(E):=\{X\in\mathbb{S}^n:\lambda(X)\in E\}\), and it is invariant under orthogonal conjugation.

notation.meaning: Eigenvalue vector in a fixed order.
Spectral lift of the eigenvalue set.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of an orthogonally invariant spectral set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric spectral sets generated by permutation-invariant subsets of eigenvalue space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be invariant under every coordinate permutation. Its spectral lift is the set \[\Lambda(E):=\{X\in\mathbb{S}^n:\lambda(X)\in E\},\] where \(\lambda(X)\) is the eigenvalue vector of \(X\) in any fixed order. Because \(E\) is permutation invariant, membership is independent of that order. Moreover, for every orthogonal matrix \(Q\), one has \(X\in\Lambda(E)\) if and only if \(QXQ^\top\in\Lambda(E)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectral set of symmetric matrices is obtained by imposing a permutation-invariant constraint on their eigenvalue vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and orthogonal-invariance statement are mathematically standard and fit Spectral Geometry, but no inspectable citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Rank Geometry
children.top_down_role: Stratified geometry induced by matrix-rank constraints.

assumptions_latex: Matrices are equipped with the Frobenius inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rank-\(r\) stratum is a smooth manifold with tangent space \(\{H:(I-UU^\top)H(I-VV^\top)=0\}\).

notation.meaning: Thin singular-vector factors of the reference matrix.
Tangent space to the rank stratum.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical fixed-rank matrix manifold formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth geometry of the fixed-rank stratum in a finite-dimensional matrix space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\mathcal M_r:=\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}X=r\}\). This is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(r(m+n-r)\). If \(X=U\Sigma V^\top\in\mathcal M_r\) is a thin singular value decomposition, then \[T_{\mathcal M_r}(X)=\{H\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:(I-UU^\top)H(I-VV^\top)=0\}.\] Its normal space is \[N_{\mathcal M_r}(X)=\{Z:U^\top Z=0,\ ZV=0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrices of fixed rank form a smooth manifold whose tangent directions cannot introduce a component between both orthogonal complements of the singular subspaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank Geometry

children.title: Spectral–Rank Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interactions between spectral multiplicity and rank strata.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}X\le r\iff\sigma_{r+1}(X)=0\iff\lambda_{r+1}(XX^\top)=0\).

notation.meaning: Ordered eigenvalues of a positive semidefinite matrix.
Matrices of rank at most r.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: singular-value characterization of matrix rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular-value and eigenvalue representations of the bounded-rank variety.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q:=\min\{m,n\}\), let \(\sigma_1(X)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_q(X)\ge0\) be the singular values of \(X\). For \(0\le r<q\), the bounded-rank set admits the spectral representations \[\mathcal R_{\le r}:=\{X:\operatorname{rank}X\le r\}=\{X:\sigma_{r+1}(X)=0\}=\{X:\lambda_{r+1}(XX^\top)=0\}.\] Since \(\lambda_i(XX^\top)=\sigma_i(X)^2\), rank geometry is encoded by the zero pattern of the spectrum of \(XX^\top\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix has rank at most r exactly when its next singular value, equivalently the corresponding eigenvalue of its Gram matrix, vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral–Rank Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singular-value and Gram-spectrum characterization is correct and appropriately classified as a representation, but no source or locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transfer of rank-dependent surrogate bounds to optimal values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An abstract infimum comparison requiring only pointwise bounds and a uniform finite rank bound over the feasible image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\ge1\). Suppose \(F_p:\mathbb S_n\to\mathbb R\) and \(\rho:\mathbb S_n\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfy \(\tfrac12\rho(X)^2\le F_p(X)\le\tfrac12\rho(X)^2(\operatorname{rank}X)^{1/p}\) for every \(X\in\mathbb S_n\). Let \(Q\ne\varnothing\), let \(A:Q\to\mathbb S_n\), and set \(\phi_*=\inf_{y\in Q}\rho(A(y))\), \(r=\sup_{y\in Q}\operatorname{rank}A(y)<\infty\), \(f_p(y)=F_p(A(y))\), and \(f_p^*=\inf_{y\in Q}f_p(y)\). Then \(\tfrac12\phi_*^2\le f_p^*\le\tfrac12\phi_*^2r^{1/p}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a matrix surrogate lies pointwise between one half the squared spectral objective and that quantity multiplied by rank to the power 1/p, then the surrogate's infimum obeys the same bounds with the uniform maximal rank over the feasible image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac12\phi_*^2\le f_p^*\le\frac12\phi_*^2r^{1/p},\qquad \phi_*:=\inf_{y\in Q}\rho(A(y)),\quad f_p^*:=\inf_{y\in Q}F_p(A(y)).

assumptions_latex: Tangent cones are taken at \(0\) using outer, inner, and Clarke-robust limits.
All example sets are closed subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both inclusions \(T_C^{\mathrm C}(0)\subset T_C^{\mathrm i}(0)\subset T_C(0)\) can be strict for closed sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The general inclusions \[T_C^{\mathrm C}(0)\subset T_C^{\mathrm i}(0)\subset T_C(0)\] need not be equalities. For \(C_1:=(\mathbb{R}\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R})\), one has \(T_{C_1}^{\mathrm i}(0)=C_1\) but \(T_{C_1}^{\mathrm C}(0)=\{0\}\). For \(C_2:=\{0\}\cup\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:2^{-2k-1}\le\|x\|\le2^{-2k},\ k\in\mathbb{N}\}\), radial gaps give \(T_{C_2}(0)=\mathbb{R}^2\) while \(T_{C_2}^{\mathrm i}(0)=\{0\}\). Thus each inclusion can be strict.

assumptions_latex: \(N_C\) denotes the limiting normal cone and \(\widehat N_C\) the regular normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(0)=\{0\}\), while \(N_C(0)\) contains both coordinate axes and nearby normal spaces switch between them.

notation.meaning: The union of the coordinate axes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal instability at a transversal union of smooth pieces.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(\mathbb{R}\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R})\). At the crossing, \[\widehat N_C(0)=\{0\},\qquad N_C(0)=(\mathbb{R}\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}).\] At a nonzero point on the horizontal axis, the normal space is vertical; at a nonzero point on the vertical axis, it is horizontal. Hence sequences approaching \(0\) through different active pieces produce incompatible limiting normal directions, and regular and limiting dual geometries disagree at the junction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At two crossing lines, nearby normal spaces alternate between perpendicular axes, while the regular normal collapses at the crossing.
