knowledge_statements.title: Switching Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent first-order branch tie that leaves branch identity to second-order curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite maximum \(f=\max_i f_i\) of \(C^2\) functions, switching degeneracy occurs at \(( ar x,w)\) when there exist distinct \(i,j\in I( ar x)\) such that
\[\langle
abla f_i( ar x),wangle=\langle
abla f_j( ar x),wangle=f'( ar x;w).\]
It is curvature-resolving when additionally
\[\langle w,
abla^2f_i( ar x)wangle
e\langle w,
abla^2f_j( ar x)wangle,\]
and curvature-persistent when these quantities are equal. In the degenerate case, first-order data alone cannot identify the locally dominant branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Switching is degenerate when multiple active branches have the same directional slope; unequal curvatures resolve the tie only at second order.

children.title: Second-Order Set Calculus

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Set Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer parabolic second-order tangent set for a closed subset of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed, let \(\bar x\in C\), and let \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\). The outer second-order tangent set to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\) is
\[T_C^2(\bar x,w):=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\,t_k\downarrow0,\ z_k\to z,\ \bar x+t_k w+\tfrac12t_k^2z_k\in C\right\}.\]
Equivalently, \(z\in T_C^2(\bar x,w)\) when
\[\operatorname{dist}(\bar x+t w+\tfrac12t^2z,C)=o(t^2)\]
along some sequence \(t\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-order tangent set contains parabolic corrections that keep a first-order tangent path feasible to order smaller than t².
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C^2(\bar x,w)\) is the set of feasible outer parabolic corrections \(z\).

notation.meaning: outer second-order tangent set in direction w

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Tangent-Normal Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-function transfer between parabolic tangents and the second subderivative of an indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and parabolically regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\in N_C(\bar x)\). For every \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\) satisfying \(\langle\bar v,w\rangle=0\), the second subderivative of the indicator obeys
\[d^2\delta_C(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=-\sigma_{T_C^2(\bar x,w)}(\bar v)=-\sup_{z\in T_C^2(\bar x,w)}\langle\bar v,z\rangle.\]
Thus the curvature-sensitive normal quantity is obtained by supporting the second-order tangent set in the normal direction, with the sign determined by the indicator-function convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under parabolic regularity and criticality, the indicator’s second subderivative is minus the support of the second-order tangent set in the normal direction.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is closed and parabolically regular at \((\bar x,\bar v)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^2\delta_C(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=-\sigma_{T_C^2(\bar x,w)}(\bar v)\).

notation.meaning: second subderivative of the indicator relative to the normal
support function of the set S

children.title: Second-Order Qualification Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Qualification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate smooth constraint showing failure of linearized and second-order feasible-set transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:g(x)=x^2\le0\}=\{0\}\) at \(\bar x=0\). Since \(g'(0)=0\), the linearized cone is
\[L_C(0)=\{w:g'(0)w\le0\}=\mathbb{R},\]
while \(T_C(0)=\{0\}\). The Mangasarian-Fromovitz and metric-regularity qualifications fail because the only active constraint gradient vanishes. Hence a second-order constraint formula cannot be applied to arbitrary \(w\in L_C(0)\); for every nonzero \(w\), no feasible parabolic arc with first-order velocity \(w\) exists. This marks the qualification boundary for transferring constraint derivatives to set geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For x²≤0 at zero, the linearized cone is all directions but the tangent cone is only zero, so unqualified second-order transfer fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_C(0)=\mathbb{R}\neq\{0\}=T_C(0)\), and \(T_C^2(0,w)=\varnothing\) for every \(w\ne0\).

children.title: Failure of Second Epi-Limits

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Second Epi-Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally Lipschitz function whose second-order quotients have phase-dependent nonconvergent epi-limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x^2\sin(\log|x|)\) for \(x
e0\). Then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and differentiable at \(0\) with \(f'(0)=0\). Its second-order difference quotients at \((0,0)\) are
\[q_t(w)= rac{f(tw)-f(0)-t\langle0,wangle}{	frac12t^2}=2w^2\sin(\log t+\log|w|)\qquad(w
e0).\]
For every fixed \(w
e0\), subsequences with phases approaching \(\pi/2\) and \(3\pi/2\) yield limits \(2w^2\) and \(-2w^2\), respectively. The locally uniform phase persistence near \(w\) prevents a single second epi-limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oscillation in logarithmic scale makes second-order quotients approach different limits along different step-size subsequences, so twice epi-differentiability fails.
assumptions_latex: Second-order quotients are taken at \((\bar x,\bar v)=(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_t\) has no unique epi-limit as \(t\downarrow0\), so \(f\) is not twice epi-differentiable at \((0,0)\).

notation.meaning: second-order difference quotient with denominator one-half t squared

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oscillatory quotient calculation is plausible and fits the failure-regime container, but no citation supports the nonexistence of a unique epi-limit. A source or inspectable formal reference is required for this nontrivial counterexample.

children.title: Second-Order Geometric Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Absent or unstable curvature-sensitive tangent geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Geometric Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed epigraph with a tangent direction but no bounded parabolic correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\ge |x|^{3/2}\},\qquad \bar x=(0,0),\qquad w=(1,0).\]
The curve \((t,t^{3/2})\in C\) shows that \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\). If \(z=(z_1,z_2)\) belonged to \(T_C^2(\bar x,w)\), feasibility of
\[\bar x+t w+\tfrac12t^2z+o(t^2)\]
would require \(\tfrac12t^2z_2+o(t^2)\ge|t+O(t^2)|^{3/2}\). Dividing by \(t^{3/2}\) gives a left side converging to \(0\) and a right side converging to \(1\), a contradiction. Therefore \(T_C^2(\bar x,w)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of |x|^(3/2) admits a horizontal tangent direction but no finite quadratic correction, so its second-order tangent set is empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\) but \(T_C^2(\bar x,w)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: outer second-order tangent set in direction w

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parabolic scaling argument is mathematically plausible and the counterexample kind fits geometric degeneracy, but the record supplies no evidence for the claimed empty second-order tangent set. An inspectable source is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Proto-Differentiability Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure is expressed by nonconvergence of graphical difference quotients of a limiting subgradient mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \((\bar x,\bar v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\). For \(t>0\), define the graphical difference quotient \(Q_t\) by \[\operatorname{gph}Q_t:=\{(h,k):\bar v+tk\in\partial f(\bar x+th)\}.\] Proto-differentiability of \(\partial f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) fails precisely when these graphs have no Painlevé--Kuratowski limit as \(t\downarrow0\), equivalently when \[\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{gph}Q_t\ne\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{gph}Q_t.\] Thus some graphical tangent behavior is not reproducible along all vanishing positive step sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proto-differentiability fails when the graphical difference quotients of the subgradient mapping have different inner and outer limits as the step tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{gph}Q_t\ne\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{gph}Q_t\).

notation.meaning: graphical difference quotient at the reference graph point

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the selected Painleve--Kuratowski characterization of proto-differentiability failure.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and graphical-limit formulation are plausible, but no citation supports the precise Painlevé–Kuratowski characterization for the limiting subgradient mapping.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Affine Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real piecewise affine functions on polyhedral pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is piecewise affine if there exist finitely many polyhedra \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\) whose union is \(\operatorname{dom}f\), together with vectors \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\) and scalars \(b_i\in\mathbb R\), such that \[f(x)=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\quad\text{whenever }x\in P_i.\] The formulas must agree at every point belonging to two pieces. Outside \(\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i\), the extended-real value is \(f(x)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise affine function equals one of finitely many affine formulas on a finite polyhedral cover of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f|_{P_i}(x)=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\) for every \(i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise affine and piecewise linear mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines continuous piecewise-affine mappings on polyhedral subdivisions and their piecewise-linear specialization on conic subdivisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous mapping \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is piecewise affine if there exist a polyhedral subdivision \(\Xi\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and finitely many affine mappings \(\{G^i\}\) such that \(\Phi\) coincides on each member of \(\Xi\) with one of the \(G^i\). It is piecewise linear when \(\Xi\) is a conic subdivision and the mappings \(G^i\) are linear. A polyhedral (respectively, conic) subdivision is a finite family of full-dimensional polyhedra (respectively, cones) covering \(\mathbb{R}^n\), such that the intersection of any two members is either empty or a common proper face of both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous mapping is piecewise affine when finitely many affine mappings describe it cell by cell on a polyhedral subdivision of the whole space. It is piecewise linear when the cells are cones and the pieces are linear. The full-dimensional cells cover the space and meet only along common proper faces, if at all.
assumptions_latex: \Xi\text{ is a finite family of full-dimensional polyhedra or cones covering }\mathbb{R}^n
P,Q\in\Xi\implies P\cap Q=\varnothing\text{ or }P\cap Q\text{ is a common proper face of }P\text{ and }Q
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi\text{ is piecewise affine (respectively, piecewise linear) when it agrees cellwise with one of finitely many affine (respectively, linear) mappings on such a polyhedral (respectively, conic) subdivision.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine and Piecewise-Affine Functions on an Open Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for real-valued functions on a bounded open set, together with the connected-domain constant-gradient characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be bounded and open. A function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ is affine if it is the restriction to $\Omega$ of an affine function on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Every such $u$ has constant gradient and can be written as $u(x)=\langle x,\nabla u\rangle+c$; conversely, when $\Omega$ is connected, a function having constant gradient is affine. A function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ is piecewise affine if it is continuous and there exist a negligible set $N$ and finitely many open sets $U_1,\ldots,U_m$ partitioning $\Omega$ with $N$, such that $u|_{U_j}$ is affine for every $j$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine function on the domain is the restriction of an affine function on the ambient Euclidean space. It has constant gradient, and on a connected domain constant gradient conversely implies affinity. A piecewise-affine function is continuous and affine on finitely many open pieces outside a negligible set.
assumptions_latex: For the converse constant-gradient characterization, $\Omega$ is connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\text{ is piecewise affine}\iff u\text{ is continuous and }\Omega=N\mathbin{\dot\cup}U_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}U_m,\ |N|=0,\ U_j\text{ open, and }u|_{U_j}\text{ affine}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conewise linear systems and trajectory well-posedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an autonomous system with a continuous piecewise-linear vector field and states the resulting global initial-value well-posedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conewise linear system is an autonomous differential equation \(\dot x=\Phi(x)\), where \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuous and piecewise linear. Such a finite continuous piecewise-linear mapping is globally Lipschitz. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diff-max piecewise-affine models and convex-regression reformulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite diff-max affine representations, the max-affine formulation of convex least-squares regression, and the nonconvex boundary of general diff-max fitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For positive integers \(k_a,k_b\), the parametric model
\[
m(x;\xi)=\max_{1\le i\le k_a}\{(a^i)^\top\xi+\alpha_i\}-\max_{1\le i\le k_b}\{(b^i)^\top\xi+\beta_i\}
\]
is continuous and piecewise affine in \(\xi\); when \(k_b=1\), it is convex in \(\xi\). For data \(\{(\xi^s,z_s)\}_{s=1}^N\), least-squares regression over convex functions is equivalent to the finite max-affine problem
\[
\min_{\{(a^i,\alpha_i)\}_{i=1}^N}\frac1N\sum_{s=1}^N\left[z_s-\max_{1\le i\le N}\{(a^i)^\top(\xi^s-\xi^i)+\alpha_i\}\right]^2,
\]
and to the convex program
\[
\min_{\{(a^i,\alpha_i)\}_{i=1}^N}\frac1N\sum_{s=1}^N(z_s-\alpha_s)^2
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
(a^i)^\top(\xi^s-\xi^i)+\alpha_i\le\alpha_s\quad(i\ne s).
\]
An optimizer yields an optimal convex regression function
\[
\widehat f(\xi)=\max_{1\le i\le N}\{(\widehat a^i)^\top(\xi-\xi^i)+\widehat\alpha_i\}.
\]
By contrast, least-squares fitting of the general diff-max model is nonconvex and does not admit the displayed linearly constrained convex formulation. The ReLU model \(\max\{a^\top\xi+\alpha,0\}\) is a special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite difference of two max-affine functions defines a continuous piecewise-affine model and is convex in the input when the second maximum has one term. Convex least-squares regression has equivalent max-affine and linearly constrained convex formulations, and their optimizer reconstructs an optimal convex regression function. General diff-max least-squares fitting is instead nonconvex. A single ReLU neuron is a special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m(x;\cdot)\text{ is continuous piecewise affine and is convex when }k_b=1;\text{ convex least-squares regression has the stated equivalent finite formulations, whereas general diff-max fitting is nonconvex.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent representations and local model of scalar piecewise affine functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous real-valued functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. The following are equivalent: (a) \(f\) is piecewise affine; (b) there exist \(I>0\), affine functions \(f_1,\ldots,f_I\), and index sets \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_I\) such that \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le I}\min_{j\in\alpha_i}f_j(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\); (c) there exist \(J_1,J_2>0\) and affine functions \(g_1,\ldots,g_{J_1}\), \(h_1,\ldots,h_{J_2}\) such that \(f(x)=\max_{1\le j\le J_1}g_j(x)-\max_{1\le j\le J_2}h_j(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). Consequently, \(f\) is directionally differentiable on \(\mathbb R^n\), and for every \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(f(x)=f(\bar x)+f'(\bar x;x-\bar x)\) for all \(x\) sufficiently near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous scalar function, piecewise affinity is equivalent to both a finite max-min affine representation and a difference of two finite maxima of affine functions. The function is directionally differentiable everywhere and locally equals its directional first-order model at every point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{(a)}\iff\text{(b)}\iff\text{(c)},\quad f\text{ is directionally differentiable, and }\forall\bar x\;\exists U\ni\bar x\;\forall x\in U:\ f(x)=f(\bar x)+f'(\bar x;x-\bar x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral-subdivision characterization of piecewise affine maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global continuous maps between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous map \(\Phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is piecewise affine if and only if there exist a polyhedral subdivision \(\Xi\) of \(\mathbb R^n\) and a finite family of affine maps \(\{\Phi^i\}_{i=1}^I\) such that, for every \(P\in\Xi\), \(\Phi|_P=\Phi^i|_P\) for at least one \(i\in\{1,\ldots,I\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous map is piecewise affine exactly when it agrees cellwise with members of a finite affine family on a polyhedral subdivision of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi\text{ is piecewise affine}\iff\exists\,\Xi,\{\Phi^i\}_{i=1}^I\text{ satisfying the stated cellwise affine representation.}

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Linear-Quadratic Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real piecewise linear-quadratic functions with finite polyhedral domains of representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is piecewise linear-quadratic if its effective domain is the union of finitely many polyhedra \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\) and, for every \(i\), there are a symmetric matrix \(Q_i\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), a vector \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b_i\in\mathbb R\) such that \[f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\quad\text{for }x\in P_i.\] On overlaps the quadratic formulas agree; outside the union, \(f\) has value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise linear-quadratic function is quadratic on each member of a finite polyhedral cover of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f|_{P_i}(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\) for every \(i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Properties of Piecewise Linear-Quadratic Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records domain, continuity, subderivative, and convex-case subgradient properties of finite-dimensional piecewise linear-quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is piecewise linear-quadratic, then \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is closed, \(f\) is continuous relative to \(\operatorname{dom}f\), and hence \(f\) is lower semicontinuous on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). For every \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the subderivative \(df(\bar x)\) is piecewise linear, \(\operatorname{dom}df(\bar x)=T_{\operatorname{dom}f}(\bar x)\), and for every \(w\) in this tangent cone, \(df(\bar x)(w)=\lim_{\tau\searrow0}[f(\bar x+\tau w)-f(\bar x)]/\tau\). If, additionally, \(f\) is convex, then \(\operatorname{dom}f\), \(\partial f(\bar x)\), and \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) are polyhedral for every \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(\partial f(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every piecewise linear-quadratic function has a closed domain, is continuous relative to that domain, and is therefore lower semicontinuous. At each domain point its subderivative is piecewise linear, has the tangent cone to the domain as its domain, and is given by the one-sided directional difference-quotient limit. In the convex case, the function domain and both ordinary and horizon subgradient sets are polyhedral, and the ordinary subgradient set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}f\text{ is closed},\quad f\text{ is continuous relative to }\operatorname{dom}f\text{ and lsc};\quad \operatorname{dom}df(\bar x)=T_{\operatorname{dom}f}(\bar x),\quad df(\bar x)(w)=\lim_{\tau\searrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w)-f(\bar x)}{\tau};\quad f\text{ convex}\Rightarrow \operatorname{dom}f,\partial f(\bar x),\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\text{ are polyhedral and }\partial f(\bar x)\ne\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent strong, strict, and isolated minimality conditions for PLQ programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order characterization of strong, strict, and isolated local minima for PLQ objectives on polyhedral sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be PLQ with polyhedral pieces $\{P^i\}_{i=1}^I$ and associated quadratics $\{q_i\}_{i=1}^I$, let $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be polyhedral, and set $\widetilde P^i=X\cap P^i$. For $\bar x\in X$, the following are equivalent: $\bar x$ is a strong local minimizer, a strict local minimizer, an isolated local minimizer, or an isolated stationary point that is a local minimizer of $f$ on $X$; the corresponding strong, strict, isolated, and isolated-d-stationary local-minimum properties hold on every active piece; $\mathrm df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)\geq0$ for all $x\in X$ and $\mathrm d^2f(\bar x)(x-\bar x)>0$ for every $x\in X\setminus\{\bar x\}$ satisfying $\mathrm df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)=0$; $\bar x$ is d-stationary and satisfies the second-order sufficient condition; and, on every active piece, $\bar x$ is d-stationary and $\nabla^2q_i(\bar x)$ is strictly copositive on $\mathcal C(\bar x;q_i;\widetilde P^i)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a PLQ objective over a polyhedral set, strong, strict, and isolated local minimality coincide and are equivalent to the stated active-piece and strict second-order conditions.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is PLQ with pieces }P^i\text{ and associated quadratics }q_i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a1)\Longleftrightarrow(a2)\Longleftrightarrow(a3)\Longleftrightarrow(a4)\Longleftrightarrow(b1)\Longleftrightarrow(b2)\Longleftrightarrow(b3)\Longleftrightarrow(b4)\Longleftrightarrow(c)\Longleftrightarrow(d1)\Longleftrightarrow(d2)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise quadratic and piecewise linear-quadratic functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite quadratic selections, with polyhedral-region compatibility in the PLQ case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal O\), and let \(\phi:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. The function \(\phi\) is piecewise quadratic on \(\mathcal D\) if there are finitely many quadratic functions \(q_1,\ldots,q_I\) such that \(\phi(x)\in\{q_i(x):1\le i\le I\}\) for every \(x\in\mathcal D\). It is piecewise linear-quadratic on \(\mathcal D\) if, additionally, there are polyhedra \(P^1,\ldots,P^I\) with \(\mathcal D=\bigcup_{i=1}^I P^i\) and \(\phi(x)=q_i(x)\) for every \(x\in P^i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous function is piecewise quadratic if each value is supplied by one of finitely many quadratic functions. It is piecewise linear-quadratic when its domain is covered by finitely many polyhedra and one specified quadratic agrees with the function throughout each corresponding polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi\text{ is PQ or PLQ precisely under the respective finite-selection and polyhedral-piece conditions stated above.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent local optimality conditions for PLQ programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local minimality of a PLQ objective over a polyhedral feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be PLQ with polyhedral pieces $\{P^i\}_{i=1}^I$ and associated quadratics $\{q_i\}_{i=1}^I$, let $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be polyhedral, and set $\widetilde P^i=X\cap P^i$. For any $\bar x\in X$, the following are equivalent: (i) $\bar x$ is a local minimizer of $f$ on $X$; (ii) for every $i\in\mathcal A(\bar x)$, $\bar x$ is a local minimizer of $q_i$ on $\widetilde P^i$; (iii) $\bar x$ is d-stationary for minimizing $f$ on $X$ and satisfies the second-order necessary condition; (iv) for every $i\in\mathcal A(\bar x)$, $\bar x$ is stationary for $f$, equivalently $q_i$, on $\widetilde P^i$, and $\nabla^2q_i(\bar x)$ is copositive on $\mathcal C(\bar x;q_i;\widetilde P^i)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a PLQ function over a polyhedral set, local minimality is equivalent to local minimality on every active quadratic piece and to the corresponding first- and second-order stationarity conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance-penalized lower-envelope representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation on a convex union of finitely many closed convex pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S=\bigcup_{i=1}^I S^i\) be convex, with each \(S^i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) closed and convex. Suppose \(\theta\) is continuous on an open set \(\mathcal O\supseteq\mathcal S\), and \(\theta=\theta_i\) on \(S^i\), where every \(\theta_i\) is \(\mathrm{LC}^1\) on \(\mathcal O\). Set \(\theta_{ji}=\theta_j-\theta_i\) and \(L_i=\max_j L_{ji}\), where \(L_{ji}\) is a Lipschitz constant of \(\nabla\theta_{ji}\). Then, for either the Euclidean- or \(\ell_1\)-distance and every \(x\in\mathcal S\), \[\theta(x)=\min_{1\le i\le I}\left\{\theta_i(x)+\operatorname{dist}(x,S^i)\max_{1\le j\le I}\|\nabla\theta_{ji}(x)\|_2+\frac{3L_i}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,S^i)^2\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous function agreeing with finitely many LC1 selections on closed convex pieces whose union is convex admits an exact lower-envelope representation. Each selection is augmented by a linear and quadratic distance penalty determined by gradient differences and their Lipschitz constants; either Euclidean or l1 distance may be used.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal S=\bigcup_{i=1}^I S^i\text{ is convex and each }S^i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
\theta:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous},\quad \mathcal O\supseteq\mathcal S\text{ open}
L_{ji}\text{ is a Lipschitz constant of }\nabla(\theta_j-\theta_i)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise Linear-Quadratic Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the finite-dimensional extended-real-valued class, including affine pieces and the required polyhedral geometry of the domain partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is piecewise linear-quadratic if \(\operatorname{dom}f=\bigcup_{i=1}^m P_i\) for finitely many polyhedral sets \(P_i\), and for every \(i\) there exist \(\alpha_i\in\mathbb{R}\), \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and a symmetric matrix \(A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) such that \(f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,A_i x\rangle+\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\) for all \(x\in P_i\). Quadratic terms may vanish, but merely having finitely many quadratic formulas on nonpolyhedral regions does not satisfy the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real-valued function is piecewise linear-quadratic when its domain is a finite union of polyhedral sets and its restriction to each set is a quadratic-affine expression with symmetric quadratic matrix. Some or all quadratic terms may be zero. A finite quadratic description on regions that cannot be arranged as a polyhedral union is not piecewise linear-quadratic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i\ \exists\,A_i=A_i^\top,\ a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \alpha_i\in\mathbb{R}:\quad f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,A_i x\rangle+\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\quad\forall x\in P_i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivatives and B-subdifferentials of piecewise-C1 maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local first-order structure of a finitely piecewise-C1 vector-valued map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^m\) be \(\mathrm{PC}^1\) near \(\bar x\), with finitely many \(C^1\) selections \(\Phi^i\) and pieces \(\mathcal P^i\). Then \(\Phi\) is B-differentiable at every point sufficiently near \(\bar x\). Moreover, \(d\mapsto\Phi'(\bar x;d)\) is piecewise linear and, for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Phi'(\bar x;d)=J\Phi^i(\bar x)d\) for every \(i\in\mathcal A'(\bar x;d)\). Its B-subdifferential is the finite set of Jacobians of selections whose active regions have \(\bar x\) in the closure of their interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finitely piecewise-C1 map is Bouligand differentiable locally. Its directional derivative is piecewise linear and is obtained from the Jacobian of any selection active along the specified direction. Its B-subdifferential consists of finitely many limiting selection Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi'(\bar x;d)=J\Phi^i(\bar x)d\quad(\forall d\in\mathbb R^n,\ \forall i\in\mathcal A'(\bar x;d)),\qquad |\partial_B\Phi(\bar x)|<\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value-function and optimizer structure for linearly perturbed PLQ minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric problem $v(c)=\min_{x\in X}\{f(x)+c^\top x\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be PLQ with polyhedral pieces $P^i$, associated quadratics $q_i$, and Hessians $Q^i=\nabla^2q_i$, and let $X\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be polyhedral. Define $v(c)=\min_{x\in X}\{f(x)+c^\top x\}$. If every $Q^i$ is copositive on $P^i_\infty$, then $\operatorname{dom}v$ is closed and convex, while $v$ is concave and piecewise quadratic on $\operatorname{dom}v$. If $f$ is strongly convex, then $v$ is PLQ on $\mathbb R^n$, and the unique optimal solution is a piecewise-affine function of $c$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Piecewise copositivity gives a closed convex finiteness domain and a concave piecewise-quadratic value function. Strong convexity gives a globally PLQ value function and a unique piecewise-affine optimizer map.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is PLQ with polyhedral pieces }P^i\text{ and Hessians }Q^i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall i,\ Q^i\text{ is copositive on }P^i_\infty\bigr]\Rightarrow\bigl[\operatorname{dom}v\text{ is closed and convex and }v\text{ is concave PQ on }\operatorname{dom}v\bigr];\quad f\text{ strongly convex}\Rightarrow\bigl[v\text{ is PLQ on }\mathbb R^n\text{ and the unique optimizer }x^*(c)\text{ is piecewise affine}\bigr]

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Active Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent geometry induced by the active polyhedra of a finite piecewise representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\operatorname{dom}f=\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i\) for finitely many polyhedra \(P_i\subset\mathbb R^n\). At \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), define \(I(x):=\{i:x\in P_i\}\). Then the Bouligand tangent cone to the domain satisfies \[T_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x)=\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}T_{P_i}(x).\] Consequently, \(d\in T_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x)\) if and only if \(d\in T_{P_i}(x)\) for at least one \(i\in I(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a domain that is a finite union of polyhedra, its tangent cone at a point is the union of the tangent cones of the pieces active at that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x)=\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}T_{P_i}(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Piece Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional second-order curvature contributed by active quadratic pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be piecewise linear-quadratic, with \(f(x)=q_i(x):=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\) on each polyhedron \(P_i\), where \(Q_i=Q_i^{\mathsf T}\). For \(x,d\in\mathbb R^n\), define \[I(x,d):=\{i:x\in P_i\text{ and there exists }\varepsilon>0\text{ such that }x+td\in P_i\text{ for all }t\in[0,\varepsilon)\}.\] For every \(i\in I(x,d)\) and all sufficiently small \(t>0\), \[q_i(x+td)=q_i(x)+t\langle Q_ix+a_i,d\rangle+\tfrac12t^2d^{\mathsf T}Q_id.\] Thus the directional quadratic coefficient supplied by piece \(i\) is \(d^{\mathsf T}Q_id\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a direction that remains in an active quadratic piece, the second-order coefficient is the quadratic form of that piece's symmetric Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_i(x+td)-q_i(x)-t\langle Q_ix+a_i,d\rangle=\tfrac12t^2d^{\mathsf T}Q_id\) for all sufficiently small \(t>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shifted Log-Sum-Exp Approximation of the Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For the nondegenerate case n at least two, this is a smoothable-function example under the stated positive-beta definition; n=1 is the exact zero-error boundary case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=\max_{1\le i\le n}x_i\) on \(\mathbb R^n\). For every \(\mu>0\), define \[h_\mu(x)=\mu\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{x_i/\mu}\right)-\mu\log n.\] For \(n\ge2\), \(h\) is \((1,\log n)\)-smoothable and \(h_\mu\) is a \(1/\mu\)-smooth approximation. When \(n=1\), the formula gives \(h_\mu=h\), the zero-error boundary case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shifted log-sum-exp function is a 1/mu-smooth underapproximation of the coordinatewise maximum with error at most mu log n. Thus the maximum is (1,log n)-smoothable for n at least two; for n=1 the approximation is exact and has zero error.
assumptions_latex: n\ge2\text{ for the stated }\beta=\log n>0\text{ convention}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h(x)=\max_i x_i\text{ is }(1,\log n)\text{-smoothable with }h_\mu(x)=\mu\log\!\sum_{i=1}^n e^{x_i/\mu}-\mu\log n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized PC1 Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local definition for vector-valued finite smooth selections; the property on a set is pointwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\) and \(x^0\in\mathbb R^m\). Then \(\alpha\) is generalized \(PC^1\) at \(x^0\) if there exist an open neighborhood \(U_\varepsilon(x^0)\) and finitely many \(C^1\) mappings \(\alpha^i:U_\varepsilon(x^0)\to\mathbb R^n\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\), such that \(\alpha(z)\in\{\alpha^1(z),\ldots,\alpha^k(z)\}\) for every \(z\in U_\varepsilon(x^0)\). Writing \(S_i:=\operatorname{Supp}(\alpha,\alpha^i)\), each \(\operatorname{int}S_i\) is connected and \(S_i\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{int}S_i)\); each contingent cone satisfies \(K_{S_i}(x^0)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{int}K_{S_i}(x^0))\); there exists \(\delta>0\) such that for every \(i\ne j\) and every unit \(r\in K_{S_i}(x^0)\cap K_{S_j}(x^0)\), some \(t_0(r)\ge\delta\) satisfies \(x^0+tr\in S_i\cup S_j\) for all \(0<t<t_0(r)\); and \(\operatorname{int}K_{S_i}(x^0)\cap\operatorname{int}K_{S_j}(x^0)=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). The mapping is generalized \(PC^1\) on \(U\) if it is generalized \(PC^1\) at every \(x^0\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is generalized PC1 at a point when it locally selects from finitely many continuously differentiable branches whose support sets and contingent cones satisfy the stated connectedness, closure, uniform ray-coverage, and disjoint-interior conditions. The property on a set is required at every point.
assumptions_latex: \(\exists\,U_\varepsilon(x^0),\alpha^1,\ldots,\alpha^k\text{ satisfying the stated selection and support-geometry conditions}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha\text{ is generalized }PC^1\text{ at }x^0\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact-line-search steepest descent can converge to a nonstationary point of a finite-max objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A failure boundary for applying ordinary gradient directions with exact line search at differentiability points of a convex, locally Lipschitz finite maximum of smooth functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
f(u,v)=\max\left\{\tfrac12u^2+(v-1)^2,\;\tfrac12u^2+(v+1)^2\right\}.
\]
For \(\delta\ne0\), set \(x_0=(2(1+|\delta|),\delta)^T\). Steepest descent using \(-\nabla f(x_k)\) and exact line search produces
\[
x_k=(2(1+|\epsilon_k|),\epsilon_k)^T,\qquad \epsilon_{k+1}=-\epsilon_k/3,
\]
so \(x_k\to(2,0)^T\). However,
\[
\partial f(2,0)=\operatorname{conv}\{(2,-2)^T,(2,2)^T\}=\{2\}\times[-2,2],
\]
and hence \(0\notin\partial f(2,0)\). Thus the limit is nonstationary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated maximum of two smooth convex quadratics, steepest descent from any initial point of the specified form, using the ordinary gradient at each differentiable iterate and exact line search, yields epsilon_(k+1) = -epsilon_k/3 and converges to (2,0). The subdifferential at that limit has first component 2, so the limit is not stationary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \epsilon_{k+1}=-\epsilon_k/3,\qquad x_k\to(2,0)^T,\qquad 0\notin\partial f(2,0)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise-linear subgradient model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of the full-memory polyhedral model formed from sampled subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and let \(X=\{x_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}\subseteq Q\). For each \(k\ge0\), choose \(g(x_i)\in\partial f(x_i)\) for \(i=0,\ldots,k\). The nonsmooth piecewise-linear model of \(f\) based on these data is
\[
\hat f_k(X;x)=\max_{0\le i\le k}
\left(f(x_i)+\langle g(x_i),x-x_i\rangle\right),
\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each nonnegative k, choose a subgradient at every sampled point through index k. The associated piecewise-linear model is the maximum, over those samples, of the affine subgradient cuts, and is defined on all of Euclidean space.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall k\ge0\ \forall x\in\mathbb R^n:\ \hat f_k(X;x)=\max_{0\le i\le k}\left(f(x_i)+\langle g(x_i),x-x_i\rangle\right)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite pointwise maxima of real-valued branch functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) and let \(f_i:U\to\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative over a compact locally convex index set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed-feasible-set specialization of marginal maximum differentiation; the admissible-direction cone is taken at each active maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X and Y be open subsets of finite-dimensional spaces, let \Omega\subset Y be compact, and define \varphi(z)=\max_{y\in\Omega}f(z,y). Fix x\in X. Suppose \Omega is locally convex at every y\in R(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in\Omega}f(x,u), and f is jointly concave on a convex neighborhood of \{(x,y):y\in R(x)\}. Then for every direction g, \varphi'(x;g) exists and \varphi'(x;g)=\sup_{y\in R(x)}\sup_{v\in\gamma(y,\Omega)}f'([x,y];[g,v]), where \gamma(y,\Omega) is the cone of admissible directions to \Omega at y; locally it agrees with the support cone of the convex localization \Omega\cap\mathcal B_r(y) for sufficiently small r.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the compact index set is locally convex at every active maximizer and the objective is jointly concave near the active graph, then the maximum function has a directional derivative in every direction. The derivative is the supremum of the objective's directional derivative over active maximizers and directions admissible for the index set at those maximizers.
assumptions_latex: X,Y\text{ are open subsets of finite-dimensional spaces}
\forall y\in R(x),\ \Omega\text{ is locally convex at }y
f\text{ is jointly concave on a convex neighborhood of }\{(x,y):y\in R(x)\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall g,\quad \varphi'(x;g)=\sup_{y\in R(x)}\sup_{v\in\gamma(y,\Omega)}f'([x,y];[g,v]).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support-function representation of a marginal derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses the derivative through supergradients of a locally concave objective, normals to the moving feasible image, and the derivative of its support function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a be closed and bounded with convex compact images, and suppose its support function a(x,\ell)=\sup_{y\in a(x)}\langle\ell,y\rangle is uniformly directionally differentiable with respect to \ell. Fix x\in X and suppose f is jointly concave on a convex neighborhood of \{(x,y):y\in R(x)\}. For every direction g, the derivative of \varphi(x)=\max_{y\in a(x)}f(x,y) exists and satisfies \varphi'(x;g)=\sup_{y\in R(x)}\min_{[\ell_1,\ell_2]\in V(x,y)}\bigl(\langle\ell_1,g\rangle+a'(x,\ell_2;g)\bigr), where V(x,y)=\{[\ell_1,\ell_2]\in\bar\partial f(x,y):\ell_2\in N_{a(x)}(y)\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed, bounded, convex compact-valued feasible mapping with a uniformly differentiable support function, and a jointly concave objective near the active graph, the marginal derivative exists. It is the supremum over active maximizers of a minimum combining the x-component of an objective supergradient with the directional derivative of the feasible image's support function, subject to the y-component being normal to the feasible image.
assumptions_latex: a(x)\text{ is convex and compact for every }x
a(x,\ell)\text{ is uniformly differentiable with respect to }\ell
f\text{ is jointly concave on a convex neighborhood of }\{(x,y):y\in R(x)\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi'(x;g)=\sup_{y\in R(x)}\min_{[\ell_1,\ell_2]\in V(x,y)}\left(\langle\ell_1,g\rangle+a'(x,\ell_2;g)\right),\quad V(x,y)=\{[\ell_1,\ell_2]\in\bar\partial f(x,y):\ell_2\in N_{a(x)}(y)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal maximum function with dependent constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the marginal function, its active maximizers, and the associated directional upper quantity under the standing Hadamard-differentiability setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X\subset\mathbb R^n and Y\subset\mathbb R^m be open, let a:X\rightrightarrows Y have compact images, and let f:X\times Y\to\mathbb R be Hadamard differentiable in both variables. The function \varphi(x)=\max_{y\in a(x)}f(x,y) is called a maximum function with dependent constraints, or a marginal function. Define R(x)=\{y\in a(x):f(x,y)=\varphi(x)\} and U(x,g)=\sup_{y\in R(x)}\sup_{v\in\widetilde K(x,y;g)}f'([x,y],[g,v]). Then the Hadamard remainder is locally uniform in the direction, the derivative of f is continuous in its direction argument, and \varphi_D^{\downarrow}(x,g)\ge U(x,g).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A marginal maximum function maximizes f(x,y) over a compact feasible set a(x) that depends on x. Its active maximizers form R(x). Under the stated Hadamard-differentiability assumptions, the directional remainder is uniform, the derivative varies continuously with direction, and the lower Dini derivative of the marginal function is at least the supremum U(x,g) over active maximizers and feasible first-order motions.
assumptions_latex: X\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ and }Y\subset\mathbb R^m\text{ are open}
f\text{ is Hadamard differentiable at every }(x,y)\in X\times Y
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi(x)=\max_{y\in a(x)}f(x,y),\quad R(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in a(x)}f(x,y),\quad \varphi_D^{\downarrow}(x,g)\ge U(x,g).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite pointwise minima of real-valued branch functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) and let \(f_i:U\to\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Their finite minimum function is \[f(x):=\min_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x),\qquad x\in U.\] Its active index set at \(x\) is \[I(x):=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}.\] If every branch is continuous, then \(f\) is continuous. Equivalently, \(-f\) is the finite maximum of the branches \(-f_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite minimum function takes the smallest value among finitely many branches; its active indices are precisely the minimizing branches.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\) and \(-f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(-f_i(x))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting Subdifferential Inclusion for a Finite Minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-subdifferential calculus for the lower envelope of finitely many extended-real-valued functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi_i:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), be finite at \(\bar x\), define \(\psi(x)=\min_{1\le i\le n}\varphi_i(x)\), and let \(M(\bar x)=\{i\mid \varphi_i(\bar x)=\psi(\bar x)\}\). If \(\varphi_i\) is lower semicontinuous at \(\bar x\) for every \(i\notin M(\bar x)\), then \[\partial\psi(\bar x)\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in M(\bar x)}\partial\varphi_i(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every branch is finite at the reference point and each inactive branch is lower semicontinuous there, every limiting subgradient of the finite minimum is a limiting subgradient of at least one active branch.
assumptions_latex: \varphi_i\text{ is l.s.c. at }\bar x\quad(i\notin M(\bar x))
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\psi(\bar x)\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in M(\bar x)}\partial\varphi_i(\bar x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial sufficient conditions for a local minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient local-minimality theorem for a generalized PC1 function at a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\) be generalized \(PC^1\), and fix \(x^0\). If either (i) \(\alpha(x^0)<\alpha_r(x^0)\) for every \(r\in\mathbb{R}^m\), or (ii) \(\alpha(x^0)\leq\alpha_r(x^0)\) for every \(r\) and \(\mathrm d\alpha(x^0;r)>0\) for every unit \(r\) satisfying \(\alpha(x^0)=\alpha_r(x^0)\), then \(\alpha\) has a local minimum at \(x^0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized PC1 function has a local minimum at x0 if every radial comparison is strictly larger there, or if every comparison is no smaller and the directional derivative is positive along every unit direction where equality occurs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^0\text{ is a local minimizer of }\alpha.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Selection Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous functions locally selecting values from finitely many smooth branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\), and let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:U\to\mathbb R\) be continuous branch functions. A continuous function \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is a finite-selection function generated by these branches if \[f(x)\in\{f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x)\}\quad\text{for every }x\in U.\] The active selection set is \(I_f(x):=\{i:f(x)=f_i(x)\}\), which is nonempty at every point. Finite maximum and finite minimum functions are particular finite selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous finite-selection function equals one of finitely many continuous branch values at every point, with the selected branch allowed to change.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_f(x)=\{i:f(x)=f_i(x)\}\ne\varnothing\) for every \(x\in U\).

notation.meaning: indices of branches selected by f at x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise continuously differentiable function and active selections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local finite-selection definition for vector-valued maps, with active-index and branch-support notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A map $z:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^q$ is piecewise continuously differentiable ($PC^1$) at $x^0$ if there are an open neighborhood $V_\varepsilon(x^0)$ and finitely many maps $z^i\in C^1(V_\varepsilon(x^0);\mathbb{R}^q)$ such that $z$ is continuous on $V_\varepsilon(x^0)$ and $z(w)\in\{z^1(w),\ldots,z^t(w)\}$ for every $w\in V_\varepsilon(x^0)$. For $x\in V_\varepsilon(x^0)$, define $I_z(x)=\{i:z^i(x)=z(x)\}$ and $\operatorname{Supp}(z,z^i)=\{x\in V_\varepsilon(x^0):z(x)=z^i(x)\}$. Each such support is closed relative to $V_\varepsilon(x^0)$, and $x\in\operatorname{Supp}(z,z^i)$ implies $i\in I_z(x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map is PC1 at a point if, on a neighborhood, it is a continuous selection from finitely many continuously differentiable maps. Active indices identify branches agreeing with the selected value, and each branch support is relatively closed in that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z(w)\in\{z^1(w),\ldots,z^t(w)\}\quad\forall w\in V_\varepsilon(x^0),\qquad \operatorname{Supp}(z,z^i)\text{ is relatively closed in }V_\varepsilon(x^0).

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Branch Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition of a finite-selection domain by active-index patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be a finite selection of functions \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:U\to\mathbb R\), and define \(I_f(x):=\{i:f(x)=f_i(x)\}\). For every nonempty \(J\subset\{1,\ldots,m\}\), define \[S_J:=\{x\in U:I_f(x)=J\}.\] The nonempty sets \(S_J\) are pairwise disjoint and partition \(U\): \[U=\mathop{\dot\bigcup}_{\varnothing\ne J\subset\{1,\ldots,m\}}S_J.\] On \(S_{\{i\}}\), one has \(f(x)=f_i(x)\). If \(x\in S_J\) and \(|J|\ge2\), then \(f_i(x)=f_j(x)=f(x)\) for every \(i,j\in J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Active-index patterns partition the domain; on a singleton pattern the selected value comes from its unique branch, while a multi-active pattern records coincident branch values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U=\mathop{\dot\bigcup}_{\varnothing\ne J\subset\{1,\ldots,m\}}S_J\).

notation.meaning: branches whose value equals the selected value at x
set of points having active-index pattern J

knowledge_statements.title: Switching Loci
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locations where a finite-selection function has more than one value-compatible branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be a finite-selection function generated by \(f_1,,f_m\), and let \(I_f(x):=\{i:f(x)=f_i(x)\}\). Its switching locus is \[\Sigma_f:=\{x\in U:|I_f(x)|\ge2\}.\] Equivalently, \[\Sigma_f=\bigcup_{1\le i<j\le m}\{x\in U:f(x)=f_i(x)=f_j(x)\}.\] Hence every switching point lies on at least one branch-equality set \(\{x:f_i(x)=f_j(x)\}\); outside \(\Sigma_f\), the selected branch index is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The switching locus consists of points where at least two generating branches equal the selected function value.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a finite selection of \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Sigma_f=\{x\in U:|I_f(x)|\ge2\}\).

notation.meaning: switching locus of the finite selection

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global weak convexity on a convex Euclidean domain with an explicit modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. For \(\rho\ge0\), the function \(f\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex on \(C\) if \[x\longmapsto f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\] is convex on \(C\). Equivalently, for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)+\frac{\rho}{2}\lambda(1-\lambda)\|x-y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is weakly convex when adding a sufficiently large nonnegative quadratic makes it convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|\cdot\|^2\) is convex on \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-function weak convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized weak convexity on a convex subset of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex and let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The function $f$ is weakly convex on $X$ if there exists a residual $r$ such that, for every $x,y\in X$ and $\tau\in(0,1)$, $$f(\tau x+(1-\tau)y)\leq \tau f(x)+(1-\tau)f(y)+\tau(1-\tau)r(x,y),$$ and, for every $z\in X$, $$\lim_{\substack{x\ne y\\x,y\to z}}\frac{r(x,y)}{\|x-y\|}=0.$$ The choice $r(x,y)=\sigma\|x-y\|^2$ with $\sigma>0$ yields the usual quadratic notion of weak convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous function is residual-function weakly convex on a convex set when its convexity inequality holds up to a two-point residual that is locally little-o of the distance between the points. A positive quadratic residual gives the usual weak-convexity definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x,y\in X,\ \forall\tau\in(0,1),\quad f(\tau x+(1-\tau)y)\leq\tau f(x)+(1-\tau)f(y)+\tau(1-\tau)r(x,y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of quadratic weak convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexification, reference-function residuals, Clarke support inequalities, regularity, and the two-sided smoothness criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The following are equivalent: (a) $f$ is $s$-weakly convex; (b) $f+\sigma\lVert\cdot\rVert^2$ is convex for some $\sigma>0$; (c) $f$ is $\varphi$-weakly convex for some $\mathrm{LC}^1$ function $\varphi$; (d) for some $\mathrm{LC}^1$ function $\varphi$, every $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $a\in\partial_C f(x)$, and $y\in\mathbb R^n$ satisfy $f(y)\ge f(x)+a^\top(y-x)-r_\varphi(y,x)$; and (e) $f+\varphi$ is convex for some $\mathrm{LC}^1$ function $\varphi$. Consequently, a $\varphi$-weakly convex function is Clarke regular. Furthermore, $f$ is $\mathrm{LC}^1$ if and only if both $f$ and $-f$ are $s$-weakly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous finite-valued function, quadratic weak convexity is equivalent to quadratic convexification, reference-function weak convexity, the stated Clarke-subgradient support inequality, and convexification by an LC1 function. Reference-function weak convexity implies Clarke regularity, and LC1 smoothness is equivalent to two-sided quadratic weak convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\Longleftrightarrow(b)\Longleftrightarrow(c)\Longleftrightarrow(d)\Longleftrightarrow(e),\quad \varphi\text{-weak convexity}\Rightarrow\text{Clarke regularity},\quad f\in\mathrm{LC}^1\Longleftrightarrow(f\text{ and }-f\text{ are }s\text{-weakly convex})

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic-residual and reference-function weak convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two specified residual forms for weak convexity on the scalar open convex domain stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open and convex and let $f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$. The function $f$ is $s$-weakly convex with modulus $\sigma>0$ when it is weakly convex with residual $r(x,y)=\sigma\lVert x-y\rVert^2$. For an $\mathrm{LC}^1$ function $\varphi$, the function $f$ is $\varphi$-weakly convex when it is weakly convex with residual $r_\varphi(x,y)=\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)-\nabla\varphi(y)^\top(x-y)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic weak convexity uses a positive quadratic residual. Reference-function weak convexity uses the first-order residual generated by an LC1 function.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R\text{ is open and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r(x,y)=\sigma\lVert x-y\rVert^2\quad\text{or}\quad r_\varphi(x,y)=\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)-\nabla\varphi(y)^\top(x-y)

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-C2 Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local lower-C^2 representation as a compactly indexed maximum of smooth functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) on an open set \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) is lower-\(C^2\) if, for every \(\bar x\in U\), there exist a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\), a compact parameter space \(T\), and functions \(\phi_t:V\to\mathbb R\) such that \[f(x)=\max_{t\in T}\phi_t(x)\quad\text{for all }x\in V,\] where \(\phi_t\) is twice continuously differentiable in \(x\), and \(\phi_t(x)\), \(\nabla_x\phi_t(x)\), and \(\nabla_{xx}^2\phi_t(x)\) depend continuously on \((t,x)\in T\times V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-C2 function is locally the maximum of a compact family of twice continuously differentiable functions with jointly continuous derivatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f|_V=\max_{t\in T}\phi_t\) with jointly continuous derivatives through order two.

notation.meaning: smooth generating function indexed by t

children.title: Quadratic Convexification
children.top_down_role: Quadratic adjustments linking local nonconvexity to convex geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex exactly when \(x\mapsto f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean quadratic convexification, allowing extended-real-valued functions.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.3 Weakly convex functions p. 214

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quadratic convexification of \(f\) with parameter \(\rho\) is the extended-real-valued function \[f_\rho(x):=f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2.\] The function \(f\) is called \(\rho\)-weakly convex, or quadratically convexifiable with modulus \(\rho\), when \(f_\rho\) is convex. Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)+\frac{\rho}{2}t(1-t)\|x-y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a quadratic of curvature rho makes the function convex; equivalently, its violation of the convexity inequality is bounded by a quadratic term.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Convexification

children.title: Prox-Regularity Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections between quadratic lower control and prox-regular behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle-\frac{\rho}{2}\|y-x\|^2\), hence \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface from global weak convexity to local prox-regularity in Euclidean space.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.3 Weakly convex functions p. 214

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexity of \(g(x):=f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\) implies that whenever \(v\in\partial f(x)\), the vector \(v+\rho x\) supports \(g\) at \(x\). Consequently, for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle-\frac{\rho}{2}\|y-x\|^2.\] In particular, this inequality holds under the local restrictions in the definition of prox-regularity at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\), so every proper lower-semicontinuous weakly convex function is prox-regular at each point-subgradient pair in its graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak convexity supplies the uniform quadratic lower support required by prox-regularity, so every point-subgradient pair of a weakly convex function is prox-regular.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regularity Interface

children.top_down_role: Functions whose convex-concave structure is expressed through an implicit representation.

assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:C\times Y\times Z\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex in \((x,y)\) and concave in \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}\sup_{z\in Z}\Phi(x,y,z)\) is represented implicitly through convex-concave saddle geometry.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a saddle-lift interpretation; the inventory locator does not expose the book's exact convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An implicit convex-concave representation of \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a formula \[f(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}\sup_{z\in Z}\Phi(x,y,z),\] where \(\Phi(\cdot,\cdot,z)\) is convex on \(C\times Y\) for every \(z\in Z\), and \(\Phi(x,y,\cdot)\) is concave on \(Z\) for every \((x,y)\in C\times Y\). The auxiliary variables are eliminated by optimization, so the resulting function need not itself be convex or concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function is obtained by eliminating auxiliary variables from a convex-concave saddle representation and may itself be nonconvex and nonsmooth.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Convex–Concave Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-Block Directional-Derivative Sum Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A blockwise decomposition for a vector-valued B-differentiable function under asymmetric semicontinuity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\psi:\mathbb R^{n+m+\ell}\to\mathbb R^k\) be B-differentiable near \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\). Suppose that for every \((d_x,d_y,d_z)\), the mapping \(\psi_x'((\cdot,\cdot,\cdot);d_x)\) is upper semicontinuous at \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\), \(\psi_y'((\cdot,\cdot,\cdot);d_y)\) is lower semicontinuous there, and \(\psi_z'((\cdot,\cdot,\cdot);d_z)\) is continuous there. Then, for every \((u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^{n+m+\ell}\), \[\psi'((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z);(u,v,w))=\psi_x'((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z);u)+\psi_y'((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z);v)+\psi_z'((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z);w).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a vector-valued B-differentiable function of three blocks, upper semicontinuity of the first partial directional derivative, lower semicontinuity of the second, and continuity of the third imply that the joint directional derivative is the sum of the three partial directional derivatives.
assumptions_latex: \psi:\mathbb R^{n+m+\ell}\to\mathbb R^k\text{ is B-differentiable near }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)
\forall d_x,\ \psi_x'((\cdot,\cdot,\cdot);d_x)\text{ is upper semicontinuous at }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)
\forall d_y,\ \psi_y'((\cdot,\cdot,\cdot);d_y)\text{ is lower semicontinuous at }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)
\forall d_z,\ \psi_z'((\cdot,\cdot,\cdot);d_z)\text{ is continuous at }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall(u,v,w),\ \psi'((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z);(u,v,w))=\psi_x'((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z);u)+\psi_y'((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z);v)+\psi_z'((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z);w)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Difference Characterization of Lower-\(\mathcal C^2\) Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence among lower-\(\mathcal C^2\), local convex-minus-smooth representations, and compact smooth-max representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every finite convex function on \(\mathbb R^n\) is lower-\(\mathcal C^2\). More generally, for an open \(O\subset\mathbb R^n\), a function \(f:O\to\mathbb R\) is lower-\(\mathcal C^2\) iff, locally around every point of \(O\), \(f=g-h\), where \(g\) is finite and convex and \(h\in\mathcal C^2\). One may take \(h\) to be a convex quadratic, even \(h(x)=\tfrac12\rho\lVert x\rVert^2\). Equivalently, locally \(f(x)=\max_{t\in T}f_t(x)\) with compact \(T\) and quadratic \(f_t\) whose coefficients vary continuously with \(t\); when \(f\) is convex, the pieces may be chosen affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite convex functions are lower-C-2. A function is locally lower-C-2 exactly when it is locally a finite convex function minus a C-2 function; the latter may be chosen as a convex norm-square quadratic. Such functions admit compactly indexed quadratic max representations, with affine pieces in the convex case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is lower-}\mathcal C^2\text{ on }O\iff \text{locally }f=g-h\text{ with }g\text{ finite convex and }h\in\mathcal C^2;\ h\text{ may be }\tfrac12\rho\lVert\cdot\rVert^2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional and Generalized Differential Calculus for ICC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional derivatives, Clarke regularity, DC structure, subdifferential containment, and conditional semismoothness for a locally Lipschitz ICC representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta\) be implicit convex-concave on an open convex set \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), with associated convex-concave bifunction \(\psi:\mathcal O\times\mathcal O\to\mathbb R\) locally Lipschitz on its domain. For every \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\mathcal O\times\mathcal O\) and \((d_x,d_y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\), \[\psi^\circ((\bar x,\bar y);(d_x,d_y))=\psi_x'((\bar x,\bar y);d_x)-\psi_y'((\bar x,\bar y);-d_y),\] \[\psi'((\bar x,\bar y);(d_x,d_y))=\psi_x'((\bar x,\bar y);d_x)+\psi_y'((\bar x,\bar y);d_y).\] Hence, for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\theta^\circ(\bar x;d)\leq\psi_x'((\bar x,\bar x);d)-\psi_y'((\bar x,\bar x);-d),\qquad \theta'(\bar x;d)=\psi_x'((\bar x,\bar x);d)+\psi_y'((\bar x,\bar x);d).\] Moreover, \(\theta\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar x\) if and only if \(\psi_y'((\bar x,\bar x);d)=-\psi_y'((\bar x,\bar x);-d)\) for every \(d\), equivalently if and only if \(\psi(\bar x,\cdot)\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\). The function \(\theta'(\bar x;\cdot)\) is DC, and \[\partial_C\theta(\bar x)\subseteq\partial_x\psi(\bar x,\bar x)-\partial_y(-\psi)(\bar x,\bar x).\] If the additional hypotheses of Lemma 4.4.5 hold at \((\bar x,\bar x)\), then \(\theta\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz ICC representation gives formulas for the bifunction's joint derivatives and corresponding identities and bounds for its diagonal function. It also characterizes Clarke regularity, establishes DC structure and a Clarke-subdifferential inclusion, and yields semismoothness under the separately referenced hypotheses of Lemma 4.4.5.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is open and convex}
\psi:\mathcal O\times\mathcal O\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex-concave and locally Lipschitz}
\text{Only for the semismoothness conclusion: the hypotheses of Lemma 4.4.5 hold at }(\bar x,\bar x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The displayed joint and diagonal derivative formulas hold; Clarke regularity has the stated equivalent conditions; }\theta'(\bar x;\cdot)\text{ is DC; }\partial_C\theta(\bar x)\subseteq\partial_x\psi(\bar x,\bar x)-\partial_y(-\psi)(\bar x,\bar x);\text{ and Lemma 4.4.5's hypotheses imply semismoothness.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Collapse of Higher-Order Lower-Smoothness Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of lower-\(\mathcal C^2\) and all higher finite or infinite lower-smoothness classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open. If \(f:O\to\mathbb R\) is lower-\(\mathcal C^2\) on \(O\), then it is lower-\(\mathcal C^\infty\) on \(O\). Consequently, for every integer \(k>2\), \[\{f:f\text{ is lower-}\mathcal C^k\text{ on }O\}=\{f:f\text{ is lower-}\mathcal C^2\text{ on }O\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower-C-2 regularity automatically yields lower-C-infinity regularity. Thus every lower-C-k class with integer k greater than two coincides with the lower-C-2 class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is lower-}\mathcal C^\infty\text{ on }O,\quad\text{and for every integer }k>2,\ \mathrm{lower}\text{-}\mathcal C^k(O)=\mathrm{lower}\text{-}\mathcal C^2(O).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local implicit solvability under uniform determinant separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence result stated using the source-defined matrix family \(\mathfrak B(y_0)\) and neighborhood \(S_{1\delta}(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\lvert\det A\rvert\ge \beta>0\) for every \(A\in\mathfrak B(y_0)\), then for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exist \(\delta>0\) and a selection \(y(x)\in\mathbb R^n\), defined for all \(x\in S_{1\delta}(x_0)\), such that \(\lVert y(x)-y_0\rVert\le\varepsilon\) and \(f(x,y(x))=0_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every matrix in the source-defined family at y₀ has determinant bounded away from zero by a common positive constant, then, for every positive tolerance, an implicit solution y(x) exists near x₀, remains within that tolerance of y₀, and satisfies f(x,y(x))=0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\delta>0\;\exists y:S_{1\delta}(x_0)\to\mathbb R^n\quad\forall x\in S_{1\delta}(x_0):\ \lVert y(x)-y_0\rVert\le\varepsilon,\quad f(x,y(x))=0_n

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coincidence-set transfer of approximate gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equality f=g is required only on the Borel set E; the conclusion holds almost everywhere on E.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}, let g be Lipschitz continuous, and let E\subset\Omega be Borel with f=g on E. Then f is approximately differentiable at almost every x\in E and \nabla_{\mathrm{app}}f(x)=\nabla g(x) for almost every x\in E.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a function agrees on a Borel set with a Lipschitz function, then it is approximately differentiable almost everywhere on that set, and its approximate gradient equals the Lipschitz function's ordinary gradient there almost everywhere.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric-matrix spectral functions generated by permutation-invariant eigenvalue functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(F:\mathbb{S}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is spectral when there exists a permutation-invariant function \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that \[F(X)=\varphi(\lambda(X))\qquad(X\in\mathbb{S}^n).\] This definition is independent of the ordering chosen for the eigenvalues. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectral function applies a permutation-invariant scalar function to a symmetric matrix's eigenvalues, equivalently producing an orthogonally invariant matrix function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transfer principle for orthogonally invariant matrix functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular-value representation, convexity transfer, subdifferentials, and proximal evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(F:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is orthogonally invariant if \(F(VXU)=F(X)\) for every \(X\) and all orthogonal \(V\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) and \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). This holds if and only if \(F=f\circ\sigma_s\) for an absolutely symmetric function \(f\), meaning \(f(Qx)=f(x)\) for every signed permutation matrix \(Q\). Moreover, \(F\) is convex if and only if \(f\) is convex. If \(F\) is convex and \(X=P\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_s(X))Q^T\) is an SVD, then \(\partial F(X)=\{P\operatorname{diag}(\mu)Q^T:\mu\in\partial f(\sigma_s(X))\}\). If \(A=P\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_s(A))Q^T\) and \(\lambda>0\), then \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(A)=P\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(\sigma_s(A)))Q^T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix function is invariant under left and right orthogonal transformations exactly when it is an absolutely symmetric function of the singular values. Convexity transfers between the functions, and subgradients and proximal points are obtained through the corresponding vector operations on the singular values.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ convex for the subdifferential and proximal formulas}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F=f\circ\sigma_s,\quad F\text{ convex}\iff f\text{ convex},\quad \partial F\text{ and }\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}\text{ transfer through an SVD}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(\varphi\) is symmetric, or permutation invariant, when \[\varphi(Px)=\varphi(x)\] for every \(x\in D\) and every permutation matrix \(P\) associated with an element of \(\mathfrak{S}_n\). Equivalently, \(\varphi(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(n)})=\varphi(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) for every permutation \(\pi\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absolutely permutation-symmetric function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines signed-permutation invariance and its equivalent characterization by sorted coordinate magnitudes; \(|x|^\downarrow\) denotes the absolute coordinate values arranged in nonincreasing order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper. The function \(f\) is absolutely permutation symmetric when \(f(x)=f(Px)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and every generalized permutation matrix \(P\in\Lambda_n^G\). This holds if and only if \(f(x)=f(|x|^\downarrow)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-real-valued function is absolutely permutation symmetric when arbitrary coordinate permutations and independent coordinate sign changes leave its value unchanged. Equivalently, its value at a vector equals its value at the nonincreasingly sorted vector of coordinate magnitudes.
assumptions_latex: \Lambda_n^G=\{P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:P_{ij}\in\{0,1,-1\}\text{ and each row and each column has exactly one nonzero entry}\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n\ \forall P\in\Lambda_n^G,\ f(x)=f(Px)\right)\iff\left(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ f(x)=f(|x|^\downarrow)\right).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-permutation invariance and decreasing rearrangement in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $N\geq1$. A function $\varphi:\mathbb{R}^N\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is symmetric if $\varphi\circ P=\varphi$ for every permutation matrix $P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical nonsmoothness mechanism for the maximum-eigenvalue spectral function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the columns of \(U_1\) form an orthonormal basis of the eigenspace associated with \(\lambda_{\max}(X)\). Then \[\partial\lambda_{\max}(X)=\left\{U_1ZU_1^{\mathsf T}:Z\succeq0,\ \operatorname{tr}Z=1\right\}.\] Therefore \(\lambda_{\max}\) is differentiable at \(X\) exactly when the largest eigenvalue is simple; in that case, if \(u\) is its unit eigenvector, \(\nabla\lambda_{\max}(X)=uu^{\mathsf T}\). Multiplicity enlarges the subdifferential from one projector to the convex set of trace-one positive semidefinite operators supported on the top eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum eigenvalue becomes nonsmooth when its top eigenspace has dimension greater than one; its subgradients are trace-one positive operators on that eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue-Induced Nonsmoothness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximum-eigenvalue subdifferential formula and simplicity criterion are mathematically standard and fit this property leaf, but they require an authoritative, inspectable source locator.

children.title: Singular-Value-Induced Nonsmoothness
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth geometry associated with singular-value multiplicity.

assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has compact singular value decomposition \(X=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\) and rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\|X\|_*=\{UV^{\mathsf T}+W:U^{\mathsf T}W=0,\ WV=0,\ \|W\|_2\le1\}\).

notation.meaning: nuclear norm, the sum of singular values

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical nonsmoothness mechanism for the nuclear norm at rank-deficient matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a compact singular value decomposition \(X=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\), \[\partial\|X\|_*=\left\{UV^{\mathsf T}+W:U^{\mathsf T}W=0,\ WV=0,\ \|W\|_2\le1\right\}.\] The free contraction \(W\) acts between the orthogonal complements of the column and row spaces of \(X\). Thus zero singular values create a nontrivial family of subgradients. In particular, the nuclear norm is differentiable at \(X\) exactly when \(X\) has full row rank and full column rank, which requires \(m=n=r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero singular values create nuclear-norm nonsmoothness through free spectral-norm-bounded subgradient components orthogonal to the matrix's row and column spaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Value-Induced Nonsmoothness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed nuclear-norm subdifferential formula is standard, but the differentiability conclusion is false for rectangular matrices: the nuclear norm is differentiable whenever X has rank min(m,n), including full-row-rank wide matrices and full-column-rank tall matrices. It does not require m=n=r. An authoritative source is also absent, so the mathematically corrected version and its locator must be supplied.

children.title: Permutation-Invariant Geometry
children.top_down_role: Orbit and stabilizer structure underlying symmetric nonsmooth functions.

assumptions_latex: \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and permutation invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\varphi(Px)=P\partial\varphi(x)\), and stabilizers of \(x\) preserve \(\partial\varphi(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivariance of convex subdifferentials under coordinate permutations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Permutation invariance implies the equivariance law \[\partial\varphi(Px)=P\,\partial\varphi(x)\] for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\) and every permutation matrix \(P\). Hence, if \(P\in\operatorname{Stab}(x)\), then \(P\partial\varphi(x)=\partial\varphi(x)\). Coordinates belonging to the same orbit of the stabilizer are geometrically interchangeable, and averaging any subgradient over \(\operatorname{Stab}(x)\) produces another subgradient fixed by that stabilizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a permutation-invariant convex function transforms with coordinate permutations and inherits every permutation symmetry fixing the base point.
knowledge_statements.title: Permutation-Invariant Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subdifferential equivariance and stabilizer-averaging claims are correct for a proper lower-semicontinuous convex permutation-invariant function and fit the property leaf, but no inspectable source is provided.
